Title: listing all the real numbers between 0 and 1
Body:
I know from Cantor's diagonal argument that the reals cannot be listed like the naturals or rationals. But consider this infinite binary tree. Let's confine things to base 2 so there are only two branches per node. Same argument works in any base I think, you just have more branches at each node making it harder to render in ascii art :)

          0.
          /\
         0  1
        /\  /\
       0 1  0 1
...and so on forever
  1. Root node has "0." on it. that's 0 with a decimal point.
  2. first level contains the first digit after decimal, so going left you get 0.0, going right you get 0.1
  3. next level contains the next digit, so from left to right you get 0.00, 0.01, 0.10, 0.11
  4. and so on forever.

To list all these reals, just go through the tree level by level and list them. Every node on the left most branch is redundant as it always gives 0. So you don't need to include the entire leftmost branch in the list, just one element is enough. There are many other redundancies: basically if you are on any node and only go left from that point on, you are only adding another zero digit, which does not change the number.

But all the others will eventually touch every real in base 2 don't they? How does this not put all the reals between 0 and 1 in a bijection with the naturals?

My guess is the problem is in step 4, the "and so on forever" part. I am not a trained mathematician, rather a former physicist so my math reasoning may be somewhat hand-wavy :)

Edit: this question is the same as Representing real numbers in $[0,1]$ with a binary tree which I did not find when writing this. However even after reading the answer to that one, I don't see where the flaw is. In that one the answer says that each real does not map to a node in the tree, rather to an infinite path from root. Seems to me I can still list them. In the listing, the reals that terminate with an infinite string of zeroes come first. I can choose the ordering in the list how I like can't I? Just like when ordering the rationals, we do it in a way that is convenient to make the bijection with the naturals obvious.

Title: Proof by contradiction and logical value

Title: Is this construction the Equilateral case of the Cramer-Castillion

Title: Conceptualizing subgaussian norms

Title: Classification of all pairs $(X, A)$ where $A$ is a retract but not a deformation retract?
Body:
Is there a structural classification of all pairs $(X, A)$ where $A$ is a retract but not a deformation retract?

Let $X$ be a topological space and $A \subseteq X$ a subspace. Recall that $A$ is a retract of $X$ if there exists a continuous map $r: X \to A$ such that $r\vert{}_A = \text{id}_A$. Recall that $A$ is a deformation retract of $X$ if there exists a homotopy $H: X \times I \to X$ such that $\forall x \in X$ and $a \in A$, $H(x, 0) = x$, $H(x, 1) \in A$, and $H(a, t) = a$ for all $t \in I$. Equivalently, the retraction $r$ is homotopic to the identity map relative to $A$.

Clearly, every deformation retract is a retract, but the converse is clearly false (for instance, consider any space $X$ with a retraction onto a subspace $A$ where the inclusion $i: A \hookrightarrow X$ does not induce an isomorphism on homotopy or homology groups, such as a space retracting onto a point that is not a path component; an example being a torus $S^1 \times S^1$ and a longitudinal $S^1$).

Are there standard geometric obstructions that neatly capture the gap between being a retract and a deformation retract?

(This may be too vague, so if it helps, I am particularly interested in whether clean conditions exist when restricted to nice categories, such as CW-complexes or ANRs).

Title: Is there any other way to compute $ \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{\sin (x+1)}{x^3+x^2+x+1} d x?$
Body:
Noticing that the integral can be expressed as a double integral, we have

$$\displaystyle \begin{aligned} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{\sin (x+1)}{x^3+x^2+x+1} d x &=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{\sin (x+1)}{(x+1)\left(x^2+1\right)} d x \\ &=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{1}{x^2+1} \int_0^1 \cos ((x+1) y) d y d x \\ &=\int_0^1 \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{\cos ((x+1) y)}{x^2+1} d x d y \\ &=\int_0^1 \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{\cos (x y) \cos y-\sin (x y) \sin y}{x^2+1} d x d y \\ & =\int_0^1\left(\cos y \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{\cos (x y)}{x^2+1} d x-\sin y \underbrace{ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{\sin (x y)}{x^2+1} d x}_{=0} \right) d y \end{aligned}\tag*{} $$

For the remaining integral, we use contour integration along anti-clockwise direction of the path $$\gamma=\gamma_{1} \cup \gamma_{2} \textrm{ where } \gamma_{1}(t)=t+i 0(-R \leq t \leq R) \textrm{ and } \gamma_{2}(t)=R e^{i t} (0<t<\pi)$$ Let $R\rightarrow \infty$, then $$\displaystyle \begin{aligned} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{\cos (x y)}{x^2+1} d x=&\Re \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{e^{-x y i}}{x^2+1} d x \\ = & \Re \oint_\gamma \frac{e^{-z y i}}{z^2+1} d z\\=&\Re\left[2 \pi i\left(\frac{e^{-y}}{2 i}\right)\right] \\ = & \pi e^{-y}\end{aligned}\tag*{} $$

Plugging back with IBP yields $$\displaystyle \boxed{ \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{\sin (x+1)}{x^3+x^2+x+1} d x=\int_0^1 \pi e^{-y} \cos y d y=\frac{\pi}{2 e}(e+\sin 1-\cos 1)}\tag*{} $$

Is there any other way to compute $ \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{\sin (x+1)}{x^3+x^2+x+1} d x?$

Title: Systems of Differential Equations with Polynomial Coefficients
Body:
First we define the differential operator $D\equiv \frac{\operatorname{d}}{\operatorname{d}\!t}$ by the linear operator on the vector space $C^\infty$ of infinitely continuous and differentiable functions by the standard general formula; $D^n(y)=y^{(n)}$.

Now consider a system of $n$ linear differential equations in $n$ unknowns of the form $$ \begin{cases} \ P_{11}(D)x_1+\cdots+P_{1n}(D)x_n=&f_1(t) \\ &\quad\vdots \\ P_{n1}(D)x_1+\cdots+P_{nn}(D)x_n=&f_n(t) \end{cases} $$ where $P_{ij}(D)$ are polynomials in the differential operator $D$. If we consider the functions as vector and the respective matrices we can rewrite it as $$ P(D)X=F. $$ Then, by using the matrix identity $$ I\det A=A\operatorname{adj} A $$ for a nonsingular square matrix $A$, we can solve the differential equation $$ \det(P(D))X=\operatorname{adj}(P(D))F $$ for each unknown function $x_{i}(t)$.

My question is this:
Why is this method not described in most ODE textbooks?
I had to go searching to find any generalization of polynomial coefficients.
What is the procedure to solve a system in this form, and why is solving the matrix equation above independently for each $x_i$ not generally accepted?

I am currently taking linear algebra and ODE separately, and I keep seeing how there is potential for so much crossover between the two subjects, but I'm having trouble finding the specific resources that tie things together.

Title: Can applying Cauchy–Schwarz too early lose a factor $M$ in a paired Kloosterman–CRT second moment?
Body:
Consider a Type-II second-moment calculation with moduli of size $Q$, coefficient indices of length $M$, and a specific arithmetic coefficient sequence $\alpha_m$ arising from a Heath–Brown decomposition.

One route estimates each completed fibre separately, takes absolute values, and then applies Cauchy–Schwarz over $m$. This gives a bound of order

$$ Q^2M^3Y^\varepsilon. $$

A different route first opens the square, retains the correlations between $m_1$ and $m_2$, and performs the paired CRT/trace calculation before applying inequalities.

Suppose that, for the particular arithmetic coefficient system under consideration, this second calculation establishes an identity of the form

$$ \mathcal V = Q\sum_{m_1,m_2\asymp M} \alpha_{m_1}\overline{\alpha_{m_2}} \sum_{q\asymp Q}\Lambda(q) K_{m_1,m_2}(q) +E_{\rm exc}, $$

where diagonal, singular and other exceptional contributions are handled separately, and the actual normalised paired kernel satisfies

$$ |K_{m_1,m_2}(q)|\ll_\varepsilon Y^\varepsilon. $$

Assume also the coefficient-mass estimate

$$ \sum_{m\asymp M}|\alpha_m| \ll_\varepsilon MY^\varepsilon $$

and an exceptional-term bound of order $Q^2M^2Y^\varepsilon$.

The trace-first route then gives the natural scale $Q^2M^2Y^\varepsilon$, rather than $Q^2M^3Y^\varepsilon$.

My question: Is the extra factor $M$ in the first route merely a possible loss from applying absolute values and Cauchy–Schwarz before exploiting the paired arithmetic structure?

In particular, once the trace identity and kernel estimate have been established for the actual coefficient system, is there any mathematical requirement to prove a stronger, universal trace identity applying to arbitrary coefficient sequences?

Title: When does a linear shift operator preserve Pascal’s recurrence?

Title: Regarding connectedness and faithfulness in Martelli's Proposition 1.5.1 on group actions.
Body:
In Bruno Martelli's Introduction to Geometric Topology, Proposition 1.5.1 states:

Let $G$ act on a Hausdorff connected space $X$. The following are equivalent:

(1) $G$ acts freely and properly discontinuously.

(2) The quotient $X/G$ is Hausdorff and the quotient map $q: X \to X/G$ is a covering map.

Martelli defines an action of $G$ on a topological space $X$ as a homomorphism

$\rho: G \to \operatorname{Homeo}(X)$.

He defines the action to be free if $g(x) \neq x$ for every non-identity $g \in G$ and every $x \in X$. Proper discontinuity is defined by requiring that, for every $x,y \in X$, there exist neighborhoods $U_x,U_y$ such that $|\{g\in G:g(U_x)\cap U_y\neq\varnothing\}| < \infty$.

  1. My main goal is to understand where connectedness of $X$ is being used in the proof.

  2. I think I have shown $(1) \Rightarrow (2)$ without using connectedness of $X$.

  3. Hence, I think connectedness of $X$ is used in proving $(2) \implies (1)$. However, while trying to prove it, I needed the action to be faithful, which is not given.

  4. Considering everything above, is Martelli implicitly assuming something?

I would appreciate clarification on whether this is an implicit convention in the text or whether I am overlooking something in the proposition.

Title: On Hermite's solution of the quintic equation
Body:
I am studying Charles Hermite's method for solving the general quintic equation using the modular equation of level 5 .

$$ u^6 - v^6 + 5u^2v^2(u^2 - v^2) + 4uv(1 - u^4v^4) = 0 $$

While reviewing this in Briot and Bouquet's Théorie des fonctions elliptiques (in the original French),

I noticed that Hermite constructs invariants using the reciprocals of $u$ and $v$: $u \mapsto 1/u$, $U \mapsto U/u^6$, so $$ U^5 + a_4 u^4 (1 - u^8) U + a_5 u^3 (1 - u^8)^2 (1 + u^8) = 0 $$

Title: What is the precise geometric relationship between the non-commutativity of $SO(3)$ and the curvature of its manifold?
Body:
I am trying to understand the geometric relationship between the non-commutativity of rotations and the curvature of the Lie group $SO(3)$.

Let $R_x(\epsilon)$ and $R_y(\epsilon)$ denote infinitesimal rotations about the $x$- and $y$-axes. Writing

$$ R_x(\epsilon)=I+\epsilon L_x+O(\epsilon^2), $$

$$ R_y(\epsilon)=I+\epsilon L_y+O(\epsilon^2), $$

we obtain

$$ R_x(\epsilon)R_y(\epsilon)-R_y(\epsilon)R_x(\epsilon) =\epsilon^2[L_x,L_y]+O(\epsilon^3). $$

For the standard generators of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$, we have

$$ [L_x,L_y]=L_z, $$

up to the choice of sign convention.

This suggests a geometric interpretation: performing infinitesimal rotations in different orders produces a residual rotation. This seems reminiscent of the failure of parallel transport around a closed loop in a curved manifold.

However, I am unsure how far this analogy can be taken. And wants to understand is there a precise geometric sense in which the non-commutativity of rotations is responsible for the curvature of $SO(3)$?

Title: Motivation for why is Möbius inversion formula... that?

$$g(n)=\sum_{d|n}f(d) \\ \Downarrow \\ f(n)=\sum_{d|n}\mu(d)g\left( \frac{n}{d} \right)$$

Why is formula for $f$ through $g$ is... whatever this is? Why are we summing function $g$ over arguments $n/d$ and then multiplying them by some random arbitrary function?

Title: Is the $dx$ in an integral expression multiplied onto the integrand?

When my teacher first introduced indefinite integrals, they told me that an indefinite integral is simply finding the antiderivative of the integrand. So I've always treated the $dx$ at the end as just another symbol — like the integral sign itself — and ignored it. Later, when I learned about integration by substitution, I found that this $dx$ can actually be used in calculations together with the integrand. Is $dx$ being multiplied by the integrand? If an integrand can be simplified into the form $f(x) = ax + bx$, should I write the integral as $\int (ax + bx)\, dx$ rather than $\int ax + bx\, dx$?From my perspective, adding or omitting parentheses affects how I recognize patterns for substitution. I feel that only expressions that appear to be multiplied by $dx$ can be treated as differentials and manipulated accordingly.

Title: Integer output from integer inputs to nested Beta functions
Body:
I know that for any positive integers $a$ and $b$, the only way for $B(a,b)\in \mathbb{Z}$ is when $(a,b)=(1,1)$, where $B(x,y)$ is the Euler beta function. This fact can be proven by contradiction after assuming that $B(a,b)$ is an integer and $a\geq b$.

Recently I have been intrigued by the complexity of rule changes to the $24$ game. The $24$ game is a game where players try to "make" the number $24$ when given a multiset of values. For example, if a player has the numbers ${1,2,3,4}$, they can make $24$ with $1\times 2 \times 3 \times 4=24$. In the process of making $24$, each number in the multi set has to be used exactly once, and the operators of $+-\times \div$ along with necessary parentheses to order operations, are allowed. Numbers in multisets are always positive integers and are usually bounded in actual games. We only allow finite multisets.

My question is, if I changed the games rules, to only allow usage of the Beta Function, would there be any multiset of hands that can possibly make 24, or any other integer greater than $1$?

Equivalently：

does there exist a finite expression formed by nesting Euler beta functions, with positive integers as the initial inputs, whose value is $24$ or any other integer greater than $1$?

Title: Why can’t conditional probability of one continuous variable with respect to another continuous variable be computed from the definition?
Body:
If I have two continuous one dimensional random variables, $X$ and $Y$, and I want to calculate $P(X < 5 | Y = 2)$, I have to first find the probability density function of $X|y$, then use it for $y = 2$, then integrate from negative infinity to $5$ with respect to $x$.

However, $$P(X < 5 | Y = 2)=\frac{P(\{X < 5\}∩\{Y = 2\})}{P(Y = 2)},$$ by the definition of conditional probability. But $Y$ is continuous, so $P(Y = 2) = 0$. So... What's going on? I can't divide by zero.

Title: Rigorousness of using parametric + polar coordinates for limits
Body:
Suppose we have a limit

$$\lim_{(x,y) \to (0,0)}\frac{xy}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}}$$

We know, via the epsilon-delta definition, that the limit evaluates to zero. However, I want to understand whether there would be other ways to also evaluate the limit. For example, I found this relation:

Take $y = f(x)$, where $f(0) = 0$. We would end up with the limit evaluating as such:

$$\lim_{x \to 0}\frac{xf(x)}{\sqrt{x^2 + [f(x)]^2}}$$

We can then use Squeeze Theorem to solve for the limit:

$$\lim_{x \to 0} -x \leq \frac{xf(x)}{\sqrt{x^2 + [f(x)]^2}} \leq\lim_{x \to 0} x = 0$$

Of course, I realized that $y$ needn't be a function of $x$, so I instead opted for polar, like so:

$$\lim_{r \to 0}\frac{r^2\sin \theta \cos \theta}{\sqrt{(r\cos \theta)^2+(r\sin\theta)^2}} = \lim_{r \to 0}\frac{r^2\sin \theta \cos \theta}{r} = 0$$

Another way that I also found involves setting $x$ and $y$ parametrically, where $x = g(t), y = h(t)$. Of course, $g(0) = 0$ and $h(0) = 0$. Then the limit becomes as such:

$$\lim_{t \to 0} \frac{g(t) h(t)}{\sqrt{[g(t)]^2 + [h(t)]^2}}$$

We can use Squeeze again, to get this: $$\lim_{t \to 0}-g(t) \leq \lim_{t \to 0} \frac{g(t) h(t)}{\sqrt{[g(t)]^2 + [h(t)]^2}} \leq \lim_{t \to 0} g(t) = 0$$

My question is, are all of these methods rigorous? Is there a scenario in which setting $y = f(x)$, polar, or parametric fail, or can they be used in place of epsilon-delta definitions?

Title: Status of the conjecture that primes are the only positive rationals with arithmetic derivative $= 1$.
Body:
In How to Differentiate a Number, Ufnarovski and Åhlander study a function $'$ on $\mathbb Q$ that they call an arithmetic derivative, defined by

  • $1'=0$;
  • $p'=1$ for any prime $p$;
  • $(ab)'=a'b+ab'$ (Leibniz rule);
  • $\displaystyle\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)'=\frac{a'b-ab'}{b^2}$ (quotient rule).

Equivalently, if $\displaystyle x=\prod_pp^{e_p}$, where $e_p\in\mathbb Z$ and only finitely many are nonzero, then $\displaystyle x'=x\sum_p\frac{e_p}{p}$.

Conjecture 12 (p. 13) of their paper states that the only positive rational solutions of $x'=1$ are the primes, and to my best knowledge, it is still unresolved. With AI assistance, I obtained a counterexample: $$x=\frac{1945086}{3125}=\frac{2\cdot3\cdot11\cdot13\cdot2267}{5^5}.$$ To show that $x'=1$, we have $$858'=(2\cdot3\cdot11\cdot13)'=429+286+78+66=859,$$ and hence $$ 1945086'=(858\cdot2267)'=859\cdot2267+858=1948211=1945086+3125. $$ Since $(5^5)'=5\cdot5^4=3125$, the quotient rule gives $$\left(\frac{1945086}{3125}\right)'=\frac{(1945086+3125)\cdot3125-1945086\cdot3125}{3125^2}=1.$$

I would appreciate any references to earlier counterexamples or other work resolving Conjecture 12.

Title: Do wreath products require a faithful action?
Body:
I'm learning about Wreath Products from Rotman's An Introduction to the Theory of Groups

They define the wreath product by introducing groups $D,Q$ and a finite $Q$-set $\Omega$. Then $D\wr Q = K\rtimes Q$ where $K=\prod_{\omega \in \Omega}D_\omega$ ($\forall \omega \;D_\omega \cong D$) and $Q$ acts on $K$ by $q(d_\omega) = d_{q\omega}$.

Then the book introduces the concept of $\Lambda\times \Omega$ being a $(D \wr Q)$-set given that $\Lambda$ is a $D$-set and introduces the actions:

$d_\omega^*(\lambda, \omega')=(d\lambda, w')$ given that $\omega=\omega'$, and otherwise acting as the identity and,

$q^*(\lambda, \omega') = (\lambda, q\omega')$

Where I have questions is when the text claims that $D \cong D_\omega^* = \{d_\omega^* :d\in D\}$ and that $Q\cong Q^*$.

As I see it this requires that both the action be faithful, which doesn't appear to be explicitly given anywhere. Does the definition of a wreath product implicitly assume that the action of $Q$ on $\Omega$ be faithful?

Tangentially, does $\Omega$ need to be finite?

Title: Does OpenAI's Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis (QRH) imply Vinogradov's least primitive root conjecture?
Body:
Definitions

Let $g(p)$ and $g^*(p)$ denote the least primitive root and least prime primitive root modulo a prime $p$, respectively. Since every prime primitive root is also a primitive root, we have

$$g(p)\leq g^*(p).$$

Thus, any upper bound for $g^*(p)$ also gives an upper bound for $g(p)$.

Vinogradov's least primitive root conjecture asserts that, for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$,

$$ g(p)\ll_\varepsilon p^\varepsilon. $$

Application of QRH to Martin's Proposition $3$

Martin's Proposition $3$, after simplifying its arithmetic factors, gives

$$ g^*(p)\ll_\sigma(\log p)^{\frac{3}{1-\sigma}}. $$

Under GRH, setting $\sigma=1/2$ yields

$$ g^*(p)\ll(\log p)^6. $$

Under QRH, setting $\sigma=7/8$ yields

$$ \boxed{g^*(p)\ll(\log p)^{24}}. $$

This bound is weaker, but does not require GRH and it implies Vinogradov's conjecture, since

$$ \boxed{g(p)\le g^*(p)\ll(\log p)^{24}\ll_\varepsilon p^\varepsilon} $$

for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$.

Questions

  1. Assuming OpenAI's claimed QRH theorem is valid, does combining it with Martin's Proposition $3$ prove Vinogradov's least primitive root conjecture?

  2. Does OpenAI's QRH paper already address Vinogradov's least primitive root conjecture?

Title: For an anima $X$, is it true that $\operatorname{Topoi}/X \simeq \operatorname{Fun}(X, \operatorname{Topoi})$?
Body:
By "category" I mean $\infty$-category. By "topos" I mean $\infty$-topos.

Let $X$ be an anima. Let $\operatorname{An}$ denote the category of animae. Then there is an equivalence $$ \newcommand\quotient[2]{{^{\Large #1}}/{_{\Large #2}}} \quotient{\operatorname{An}}{X} \simeq \operatorname{Fun}(X, \operatorname{An}) $$ This equivalence works as follows:

In one direction, for $Y \longrightarrow X$, we obtain a functor $X \longrightarrow \operatorname{An}$ by sending $x \in X$ to the fiber $Y_x$, sending a path $p: x_1 \longrightarrow x_2$ to the parallel transport map $Y_{x_1} \overset{\simeq}{\longrightarrow} Y_{x_2}$, etc. .

In the other direction, for a functor $F: X \longrightarrow \operatorname{An}$, we define a space $Y$ as the integral or colimit $$ Y = \underset{x \in X}{\operatorname{colim}} F(x) $$ Then $Y$ has a canonical map back to $X$.

As a concrete example, if $X = BG$, then this says that animae over $BG$ are the same as animae with a $G$-action.

Now let $\operatorname{Topoi}$ denote the category of topoi with geometric morphisms. Let $X$ be an anima. Since animae embed fully faithfully into topoi by sending $X$ to $\quotient{\operatorname{An}}{X}$, we may also consider $X$ as a topos.

Question: Is it true that we have the following equivalence? $$ \quotient{\operatorname{Topoi}}{X} \simeq \operatorname{Fun}(X, \operatorname{Topoi}) $$

Title: How is the smoothness of maps between Frechet spaces defined? (regarding Bismut's family index theorem)
Body:
I'm reading "Heat Kernels and Dirac Operators" by Berline,Getzler,and Vergne.

In the chapter 9 of this book,to explain Bismut's family index theorem, they consider an "Frechet vector bundle." More precisely, let $ \pi : M \to B$ be a fiber bundle with compact manifold fibers, and let $\mathcal{E}$ be a superbundle on M, and $|\Lambda_{\pi}|$ be the vertical density bundle. Then define an infinite-dimensional vector "bundle" $\pi_*\mathcal{E}$ over B by setting $(\pi_*\mathcal{E})_z := \Gamma(M_z , \mathcal{E}_z \otimes |\Lambda_{M_z}|^{1/2})$. These fibers can be seen as Frechet spaces.

In order to define a fiber bundle, we must fix a model fiber and make trivializations. Certainly, this can be accomplished by focusing on each components of B, as the authors say in Lemma 9.9. Fix a point $z_0 \in B$, and take model fibers $M_0$ of M and $E_0$ of E on the neighborhood U of $z_0$. Then by considering paths that connects $z_0$ and points of B around which M is trivialized, we can take a fixed fiber $\Gamma(M_0 , \mathcal{E}_0 \otimes |\Lambda_{M_0}|^{1/2}) \times U$ (although the trivialization may depend on the choice of paths). So, the only remaining problem is the smoothness of transition maps between two Frechet spaces.

However,the authors did not define the smoothness of maps between Frechet spaces, though they probably use it.

So my question is: How can we define the smoothness of maps between two Frechet space? Or how can we define the smoothness of maps from an open set of Euclid spaces to the spaces of maps between Frechet spaces?

Title: Why isn’t the axiom of choice disproved using proof by contradiction?
Body:
Proof by contradiction tends to proceed using the following pattern.

  1. Assume $A$, the negation of the statement we want to prove.
  2. Then $A$ implies $B$.
  3. But $B$ causes a contradiction.
  4. Therefore, $A$ must not be true, meaning our statement must be true.

When we assume the axiom of choice, we get some wild implications. Why isn’t that seen as a proof by contradiction?

Title: Is swapping the order of $e^{-\partial^{2}}$ and the sum in $\sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} t^{n} x^{n}$ valid?
Body:
I was looking into some results on orthogonal polynomials and noticed a fairly recent result on the ordinary generating function of the Hermite polynomials, namely at https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.16209. However, I have doubts about the validity of the main result, in part because of how it was submitted (independent researcher never instills the most confidence, and of all the fields this paper could fall under, all it was given was math.gm), but also because some of the operations used feel questionable. The big one is the one labeled as Eqn. 4:

$$ g(t, x) = e^{-\frac{\partial_{x}^{2}}{2}} \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} t^{n} x^{n} = \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} t^{n} H_{n}(x) = e^{-\frac{\partial_{x}^{2}}{2}} \left( \frac{1}{1 - x t} \right) $$

with the third term giving the generating function, but that requires passing the operator inside the summation. Now I know about the results discussed in Can one differentiate an infinite sum?, but I don't know how well those compose with an infinite sum of differential operators. Moreover, the sum used here with $t^{n} x^{n}$ is only pointwise convergent, so one can't say anything along the lines of uniform convergence keeps all operations valid.

I know the standard tools that come up when considering swapping operations are things like the Dominated Convergence Theorem, the Monotone Convergence Theorem, Fubini's Theorem, and the Leibniz Integration Rule. A combination of the last 2 seems like they could work here, but I can't figure out the details.

Thanks for any help and insights.

Title: Is the composition of regular monomorphisms a regular monomorphism?
Body:
I would like to have a generalized definition of embeddings in an arbitrary category, or at least in some large class of categories. These generalized embeddings should be morphisms such that

  • they are monomorphisms,
  • they are closed under composition,
  • they correspond to usual embeddings in topological spaces and groups.
  • they are "isomorphisms to image".

An article in nLab proposes regular monomorphisms as a possible formalization of embeddings, and shows how to formalize the idea of being "isomorphism to image".

A regular monomorphism in a given category is a morphism $f: X \to Y$ which is an equalizer of some pair of parallel morphisms $g_0, g_1: Y \to Z$, i.e. $g_0 \circ f = g_1 \circ f$ and $f$ is universal with this property. In the category of topological spaces, regular monomorphisms are exactly the embeddings. In the category of groups, every monomorphism is regular, so that monomorphisms = regular monomorphisms = embeddings.

Perhaps this is just my inexperience with categories, but I cannot answer this:

Is the composition of regular monomorphisms a regular monomorphism in any category?

If not, is there a way to "fix" this, either by a "better" definition, or by restricting the class of categories?

Title: Is this a valid proof that every $4\times n$ rectangle with $n\ge 11$ can be tiled by I-trominoes and Z-tetrominoes?
Body:
I was looking at OEIS A397850, which counts tilings of a $4\times n$ rectangle using straight trominoes and Z-tetrominoes, allowing rotations and reflections.

The OEIS entry notes empirically that tilings seem to exist for every $n\ge 11$.

I noticed the following simple argument.

There are tilings for $4\times11$, $4\times12$, and $4\times13$.

Also, a $4\times3$ rectangle can clearly be tiled using four straight trominoes.

Therefore, given any tiling of a $4\times n$ rectangle, we can attach a tiled $4\times3$ rectangle to its side and obtain a tiling of a $4\times(n+3)$ rectangle.

Thus we get tilings for

$$11+3k,\qquad 12+3k,\qquad 13+3k$$

for every integer $k\ge0$.

Since every integer $n\ge11$ belongs to one of these three residue classes, it follows that every $4\times n$ rectangle with $n\ge11$ is tileable.

So my questions are:

  1. Is this argument a complete and valid proof?
  2. Is this result already known somewhere in the literature?
  3. If it is correct and not already referenced, would it be appropriate to add this proof to OEIS A397850?

I also investigated a related question concerning the minimum number of Z-tetrominoes required. A finite-state exhaustive search suggests that a tiling using exactly one or exactly two Z-tetrominoes is impossible. I am still checking this part carefully, so I am mainly asking about the simpler existence proof above.

Title: Alternative method to calculate $\int_0^1\int_0^x\int_{x-y}^{x+y}\Delta(x,y,z)dzdydx=\frac{17-6G}{240}$
Body:
In my previous, 2 month old question, I wanted to calculate below integral $$I:=\int_0^1\int_0^x\int_{x-y}^{x+y}\Delta(x,y,z)dzdydx$$ where $\Delta(x,y,z)$ is area of triangle with side length $x,y,z.$

The approach I took was to dehomogenize $\Delta$ and use cosine law to get $I=\frac{1}{10}\int_0^1u^2J(u)du$ when $$J(u):=\int_0^\pi\frac{\sin^2\theta}{\sqrt{1+u^2-2u\cos\theta}}d\theta$$ and use elliptic integrals to calculate $J(u)$. I got $J(u)=\frac{2}{3u^2}\left((1+u^2)E(u)-(1-u^2)K(u)\right)$ and Finally $I=\frac{17-6G}{240}$ when $G$ is Catalan's constant.

I submitted this problem to the "Integration of the Week" at my school (which I organize) and received an unexpected alternative answer, which posted as self-answer of this question.

I naturally came to think that a third solution might exist. What new solutions might there be? Any kind of help is graceful.

Title: Estimating the $L^q$ norms for the increments $X - \mathbb{E}[X \ | \ \mathcal{F}]$
Body:
Suppose I'm given some estimate on the $L^q$ norm of a random variable: $\mathbb{E}[|X|^q]^{1/q} \leq C$, $q \geq 1$. Now consider a $\sigma-$algebra $\mathcal{F}$ with respect to which $X$ is not measurable. Is there some way to employ the above inequality to give an estimate to $\mathbb{E}[|X - \mathbb{E}[X \ | \mathcal{F}]|^q]^{1/q}$? The simplest thing is of course to simply employ the Minkowski inequality and observe that due to Jensen and the fact that $q \geq 1$:

\begin{equation} \Vert X - \mathbb{E}[X \ | \ \mathcal{F}]\Vert_q \leq \Vert X \Vert_q + \mathbb{E}[|\mathbb{E}[X \ | \ \mathcal{F}]|^q]^{1/q} \leq C + \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[|X|^q \ | \ \mathcal{F}]]^{1/q} \leq 2C \end{equation}

so that we do have some bound. I was however wondering whether some sharper bound could be attained that made use of the particular form of the difference

Title: A universal doubling construction for directed terraces in $\mathbb{Z}_{2m}$
Body:
Directed terraces of cyclic groups are well understood for odd orders (e.g., Walecki’s construction), but for even orders no general doubling principle seems to be known. I prove that for any directed terrace $$T_m$$ of even order $m$, one can explicitly construct a terrace $T_{2m}$ such that under the quotient projection $$ \pi : \mathbb{Z}_{2m} \to \mathbb{Z}_m, $$ the lifted terrace satisfies $$ \pi(T_{2m}) = \big(\mathrm{rev}(T_m + m/2),\; T_m + m/2\big). $$

This yields a universal quotient-self-similarity and induces a canonical $2\times 2$ block structure in the associated Latin square. Iterating the construction produces a hierarchy $$ T_m,\; T_{2m},\; T_{4m},\; T_{8m},\ldots $$ with stable recursive structure.

I would be interested in any prior references to similar doubling principles, or related structural results for terraces or complete Latin squares.

Title: Is $k^6 - 1$ a congruent number for every positive even integer $k$?
Body:
I propose the following conjecture.

Conjecture. For every positive even integer $k$, the number

$$ n = k^6 - 1 $$

is a congruent number.

That is, for every positive even integer $k$, there exists a right triangle with rational side lengths and area $k^6 - 1$.

Equivalently, there exist positive integers $x,y,z,t$ such that

$$ x^2 + ny^2 = z^2 $$

and

$$ x^2 - ny^2 = t^2, $$

where $n = k^6 - 1$.

Question: Is this conjecture true for every positive even integer $k$? If so, is there a general proof or an explicit construction of such a right triangle?

Title: Are all primorials congruent numbers?
Body:
Recall that a positive integer $n$ is called a congruent number if it is the area of a right triangle with three rational side lengths. Equivalently, there exist positive integers $x,y,z,t$ such that

$$ x^2+ny^2=z^2 \qquad\text{and}\qquad x^2-ny^2=t^2. $$

Let $p_k$ denote the $k$-th prime, and let $p_k\#$ denote the $k$-th primorial:

$$ p_k\#=\prod_{j=1}^{k}p_j. $$

Using Tunnell's theorem, I have numerically checked the necessary condition for congruence for several initial primorials. The values I tested are

$$ \begin{aligned} p_2\# &= 6,\\ p_3\# &= 30,\\ p_4\# &= 210,\\ p_5\# &= 2310,\\ p_6\# &= 30030,\\ p_7\# &= 510510,\\ p_8\# &= 9699690. \end{aligned} $$

The first few of these numbers are known to be congruent. In particular, $210$ is explicitly listed as a congruent number in R. Alter and T. B. Curtz, A Note on Congruent Numbers, Mathematics of Computation 28 (1974), 303–305.

This leads me to the following conjecture.

Conjecture. Every primorial $p_k\#$ with $k\ge 2$ is a congruent number.

I have the following questions:

  1. Is this conjecture already known, or has it been settled in the literature?

  2. If the conjecture is true, is there a direct or explicit proof, perhaps by constructing rational right triangles or by using genus theory or $2$-descent, rather than relying on Tunnell's criterion together with the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture?

  3. Is there a heuristic reason to expect this pattern eventually to fail for some larger primorial? In particular, can the ranks or other arithmetic properties of the elliptic curves

    $$ E_n:\quad y^2=x^3-n^2x, \qquad n=p_k\#, $$

    shed light on this question?

Title: Asymptotic density of the set of gapless positive integers.
Body:
Let $n$ be a positive integer. I define $n$ to have the property of being gapless if, for any prime numbers $p$ and $p'$ that divide $n$, every prime number $p''$ in between $p$ and $p'$ also divides $n$. For example, $30 = 2 \times 3 \times 5$ is a gapless positive integer, but neither $10 = 2 \times 5$ nor $14 = 2 \times 7$ is a gapless positive integer. Of course, every prime number and every power of a prime number is gapless.

My question is, what is the asymptotic density of the set of gapless positive integers within the set of positive integers? Does it even have an asymptotic density? I conjecture that the asymptotic density is $0$.

Title: Computation of structure constants of a Lie Algebra
Body: On page 154 of "Analysis, Manifolds and Physics", the process of computing the structure constants of a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{G}$ is described. Starting from the Lie bracket of two left invariant vector fields of the algebra:$$ \begin{aligned} &\left[v_a, v_\beta\right]=f^\gamma_{a\beta}v_\gamma \iff \\ &v_a^\kappa(g)\frac{\partial v_\beta^\lambda(g)}{\partial g^\kappa}-v_\beta^\kappa(g)\frac{\partial v_a^\lambda(g)}{\partial g^\kappa}=f^\gamma_{a\beta}v_\gamma^\lambda(g) \end{aligned}$$ Then knowing that $$v_\beta^\lambda(g)=\left.\frac{dL^\lambda(g,h)}{dt}\right|_{t=0}=\left.\frac{\partial L^\lambda(g,h)}{\partial h^\mu}\right|_{h=h(0)}\left.\frac{dh^\mu}{dt}\right|_{t=0}=\left.\frac{\partial L^\lambda(g,h)}{\partial h^\mu}\right|_{h=e}\gamma_\beta^\mu$$ Where $L^\lambda(g,h)=(gh)^\lambda$ is the coordinate representation of the product of two elements of the Lie group and $\gamma_\beta^\mu=v_\beta^\mu(e)$. Setting $g=e$ we get: $$\gamma_{\beta}^\mu\gamma_{a}^\kappa\left.\frac{\partial^2 L^\lambda(g,h)}{\partial g^k\partial h^\mu}\right|_{g=h=e}-\gamma_{a}^\mu\gamma_{\beta}^\kappa\left.\frac{\partial^2 L^\lambda(g,h)}{\partial g^k\partial h^\mu}\right|_{g=h=e}=f_{a\beta}^\gamma\gamma_\gamma^\lambda$$Then the book claims that the coordinates of $\gamma_\gamma^\lambda$ are $\delta^\lambda_\gamma$, and arrives at the final result of:$$\boxed{f_{a\beta}^\gamma=\left(\frac{\partial^2 L^\gamma(g,h)}{\partial g^a\partial h^\beta}-\frac{\partial^2 L^\gamma(g,h)}{\partial g^\beta\partial h^a}\right)_{g=h=e}}$$I don't understand why the action of a left invariant vector field would act on the identity $e$ and give coordinates of a Kronecker delta. I am also confused by the indices $\gamma_\gamma^\lambda$, since from what I understand this is meant to be a tangent vector at the identity, yet it has two free indices. Any help is welcome.

Title: A Stieltjes integral formula for a logarithmic derivative
Body:
Let $g(t)=\cosh t\ln(2\cosh t)-t\sinh t$ and $F(x)=-g'(\sqrt{x})/(\sqrt{x}\,g(\sqrt{x}))$ for $x>0$.

Is there an explicit function $\rho(s)\ge0$ satisfying $$ F(x)=\int_{\pi^2/4}^{\infty}\frac{\rho(s)}{x+s}\,ds \tag{1}\label{1} $$ for all $x>0$?

Attempt. We have $g''(t)=g(t)-\operatorname{sech}t$ and $F(x)=\operatorname{sech}(\sqrt{x})/g(\sqrt{x})-\tanh(\sqrt{x})/\sqrt{x}$. Also, $\lim\limits_{x\to0^+}F(x)=1/\ln2-1$ and $\lim\limits_{x\to\infty}\sqrt{x}\,F(x)=1$.

If $\eqref{1}$ holds, then $(-1)^kF^{(k)}(x)=k!\int_{\pi^2/4}^{\infty}\rho(s)(x+s)^{-k-1}\,ds>0$ for every $k\ge0$.

Title: An asymptotic formula for $c_n^*/b_n^*$
Body:
Let $g(t)=\cosh t\ln(2\cosh t)-t\sinh t$ and $J_n(b,c)=(bc)^{n/2}\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}g\left((k-n/2)\ln(b/c)\right)$. For $n\ge7$, consider $$ (a_n^*,b_n^*,c_n^*) =\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\substack{a+b+c=1\\a>0,\ b>c>0}} (1-a^n-b^n-c^n) e^{\frac{n(a^n\ln a+b^n\ln b+c^n\ln c)-J_n(b,c)} {1-a^n-b^n-c^n}}. \tag{1}\label{1} $$

My conjecture is that $$ \color{blue}{\frac{c_n^*}{b_n^*} =\frac14e^{(3\ln n-\kappa_\varepsilon+o(1))/n}, \tag{2}\label{2}} $$ where $\varepsilon=0$ for even $n$ and $\varepsilon=1/2$ for odd $n$, with $$ \kappa_\varepsilon =2\ln\left( \frac{3}{\sqrt{2\pi}\ln(9/4)} \sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}g((j+\varepsilon)\ln4) \right). $$ Can $\eqref{2}$ be proved?

Attempt. For $t=\ln(b/c)$, the Fourier transform of $g$ implies $$ J_n(b,c)=(bc)^{n/2}\left[ 2^n\int_0^\infty \frac{\cos^n(tu/2)}{(1+u^2)\cosh(\pi u/2)}\,du -2g(nt/2) \right]. $$ The infinite sums in $\kappa_\varepsilon$ have elliptic-integral expressions in this answer, but I have not deduced $\eqref{2}$ from this identity.

Title: What is the mathematical intuition and historical motivation behind the Faedo–Galerkin method for nonlinear PDEs?
Body:
Consider the nonlinear parabolic equation

$$ \begin{cases} u_t-\Delta u=|u|^{p-2}u, & (x,t)\in\Omega\times(0,T),\\ u=0, & (x,t)\in\partial\Omega\times(0,T),\\ u(x,0)=u_0(x), & x\in\Omega, \end{cases} $$

where $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ is a bounded domain and $p>2$.

In the Faedo–Galerkin method, we choose a suitable basis $\{w_j\}_{j\geq 1}$ of $H_0^1(\Omega)$ and construct approximate solutions of the form

$$ u_m(x,t)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}c_{mj}(t)w_j(x). $$

This leads to a finite-dimensional system of ordinary differential equations:

$$ \begin{aligned} &(u_m'(t),w_j) +(\nabla u_m(t),\nabla w_j)\\ &\qquad=(|u_m(t)|^{p-2}u_m(t),w_j), \quad j=1,\ldots,m. \end{aligned} $$

After establishing uniform a priori estimates independent of $m$, we attempt to extract a subsequence and pass to the limit as $m\to\infty$ to obtain a weak solution $u$.

Why did mathematicians originally consider approximations of the form

$$ u_m(x,t)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}c_{mj}(t)w_j(x) $$

instead of directly seeking a solution in an infinite-dimensional function space?

I am especially interested in the reasoning that led to this construction, rather than the technical details of the convergence proof. I would also appreciate references discussing the historical development of this idea and its relationship to other existence methods.

Title: Baby Rudin Theorem 2.34 (Is my interpretation correct?)
Body:
Theorem: Compact Subsets of metric spaces are closed I struggled a bit with this proof and wanted to see if my interpretation of Rudin's proof is proper.

Proof: Let $K$ be a compact subset of a metric space X. Proving $K$ is closed is logically equivalent to proving $X\setminus{K}=K^c$ is open.

Let $p\in K^c$. If $q\in K$, let $$\epsilon = \frac{1}{2} d(p,q) $$ Then, if $W_\epsilon(q)=N_\epsilon(q)$ and $V_\epsilon(p)=N_\epsilon(p)$, $$W_\epsilon(q)\cap V_\epsilon(p)=\emptyset$$ Since every open cover of $K$ has a finite subcover, we know there exists a finite number of points $q_k$ such that $$K\subset W_{\epsilon_1}(q_1)\cup\cdots \cup W_{\epsilon_n}(q_n), \quad \text{for }k\in \{1,\ldots,n\} \text{ and } \epsilon_k=\frac{1}{2}d(p,q_k)$$ Then, taking $\epsilon_\min=\min_k \epsilon_k$ gives, $$V_{\epsilon_\min}(p)\cap \bigcup_{k}W_{\epsilon_k}(q_k)=\emptyset$$ Thus, $V_{\epsilon_\min}(p)\subset K^c$. In other words, every point $p\in K^c$ is an interior point of $K^c$ therefore $K^c$ is an open subset of $X$. Thus, $K$ is closed.

I know this is very similar to Rudin's proof but I wanted to know if it still worked given that it was more understandable to me. Thank you!

Title: What line separates descriptive statistics from inferential statistics?

So... in this situation, technically, I'm doing inferential statistics... right? Or maybe not. Maybe the fact that I don't have a margin of error and a confidence interval turns the information useless (because I don't know how accurate the mean is), so I'm not actually making any statements about the population?

So, my question is: why doesn't descriptive statistics help me make statements about a population (inferential statistics), even though a representative sample of the population is being used? What line separates descriptive statistics from inferential statistics, that makes one capable of making statements about a population, but the other not, even though both use a representative sample of the population?

Title: Prove that any $k$-edge hypergraph of order $n$ having the size of any linear-order subgraph not greater than the order would have linear size
Body:
Given positive integers $k, n \; (k \ge 2)$ ($k$ is fixed) and a (fixed) constant $c \in \left [ \frac{1}{2}, 1 \right )$.

Consider simple $k$-edge-only hypergraphs (called $k$-graph for short). Define a class of $k$-graph: $$H_k(n, c) := \left \{ G \; | \; V(G) = \{ 1, ..., n \} \; \text{ and } \; \forall V \subseteq V(G), \; |V| \le c \cdot n \; \rightarrow \; |E(G(V))| \le |V|\right \}$$

whereas $V(\cdot)$ is the vertex set and $G(V)$ is the induced subgraph of $G$ from the vertex subset $V$ and $E(\cdot)$ is the edge set.

To put it simply, $H_k(n,c)$ is the class of all $k$-graphs of order $n$ satisfying that each of its induced subgraphs of order not greater than $c \cdot n$ has the number of edges not greater than the number of vertices. With $k=2$, such subgraphs would have either no cycle or only 1 simple cycle.

The problem: prove or disprove the following $$\exists n_0 \in \mathbb{N}, \; \exists A > 0, \; \forall n \ge n_0, \; \forall G \in H_k(n, c), \; |E(G)| \le A \cdot n$$

To put it simply, the statement means that, with large enough $n$, the size of any graph in $H_k(n,c)$ is $O(n)$. With $k = 2$, this is relatively easy to prove to be correct.

Title: Solving a real integral through residue theorem
Body:
Consider the integral $$I=\int_0^\infty \frac{x^up^{x}\Gamma(ax+b)}{q^{ax}\left(\Gamma(x)\right)^n}\mathrm dx,$$ where $n\ge 0,u\ge 0,b\ge 1\in \mathbb{N}$ and $a>0$ such that $a\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ (irrational), $x,p,q>0$. The parameters can be chosen so that the integral exists.

To use the residue theorem we regard the integral as an integral in the complex plane, replacing $x$ by $z$. We need to find the poles of $\Gamma(az+b)$, as well as the zeros of $1/\Gamma(z)^n$ that might cancel some the poles, but making $a$ irrational we avoid this extra problem. The poles are $$ z_k=-\frac{b+k}{a},\,\,k=0,1,... $$

Now the problem is to find a proper contour which embraces the poles, but these lie in the real line, so I am having difficulties to follow. Any help would be great, thanks in advance.

Title: Cauchy Completion of Riemann Integrable Functions
Body:
I was recently introduced to the following example of a sequence of Riemann integrable functions which converges (absolutely) to a non-Riemann integrable function in my measure theory course:

Let $\mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1] = \{q_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be some enumeration. Then define $f_n := \chi_{\{q_1, \ldots , q_n\}}$ to be the characteristic function of the first $n$ terms of our enumeration. Each $f_n$ is Riemann integrable, but our sequence converges to the Dirichlet function, which is known to be non-Riemann integrable.

This demonstrates that Riemann integrable functions are not Cauchy complete (with respect to usual distance). The following questions I think are then natural to ask:

  1. What is the Cauchy completion of Riemann integrable functions with respect to usual distance? Is it just Lebesgue integrable functions, or is it something more?
  2. What is the Cauchy completion with respect to other metrics? What sort of spaces do you get?
  3. What is the "smallest" class of integrable functions which is Cauchy complete?

Title: Last non-zero digit of $((2026)!)!)!$
Body:
Denote $D(n)$ as the last non-zero digit of $n!$. I am looking for an optimal numerical method to compute the last non-zero digit of large nested factorials such as $D((2026!)!)=((2026)!)!)!$. The standard recurrence for computing $D(n)$, writing $n=5q+r$ with $0\le r<5$, is $$D(n)\equiv D(q)D(r)2^q\pmod{10}$$ with initial values $D(0),\ldots,D(4)=1,1,2,6,4$, so in code it would look something like the following:

def D(n):
    small = (1, 1, 2, 6, 4)
    powers_of_two = (6, 2, 4, 8)
    result = 1
    while n >= 5:
        q, r = divmod(n, 5)
        result = result * small[r] * powers_of_two[q % 4] % 10
        n = q

    return result * small[n] % 10

The above code does work for two nested factorials, such as $D(2026!)=6$. However, for three factorials, the input to this function would be $((2026!)!)$, which I can't compute in code. I saw a similar but more challenging problem here. It is asking to compute the last non-zero digit by hand (which I am not sure is even possible). Is there a way to exploit the fact that the input in the function $D(n)$ is itself is a factorial?

Addendum: The sequence $a_k=D(k)$ is listed as OEIS A008904. The site mentions that the decimal number obtained by concatenating its terms, $\alpha=0.a_0a_1a_2\cdots=0.1126422428\cdots,$ is transcendental. Therefore, the nested factorials select a subsequence of these digits.

Title: When does a faithful right adjoint have a regular epimorphic counit?
Body:
Let $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ and $G:\mathcal D\to\mathcal C$ be functors forming an adjunction $F\dashv G$, with counit

$$ \varepsilon:FG\Rightarrow 1_{\mathcal D}. $$

It is well known that $G$ is faithful if and only if every component

$$ \varepsilon_D:FG(D)\to D $$

is an epimorphism.

I am interested in strengthening this result by requiring the components of the counit to be regular epimorphisms.

More precisely, I would like to ask:

  1. Under what additional assumptions on $\mathcal D$, or on the adjunction $F\dashv G$, does the faithfulness of $G$ imply that every component $\varepsilon_D$ is a regular epimorphism?

  2. Are there interesting counterexamples, particularly in algebraic categories?

  3. Is there a known characterization of adjunctions satisfying this stronger condition?

For example, the implication holds if every epimorphism in $\mathcal D$ is regular. I am particularly interested in conditions that do not require this property for all epimorphisms.

I am aware of the paper by G. M. Kelly and A. Power, Adjunctions whose counits are coequalizers, and presentations of finitary enriched monads (Journal of Pure and Applied Algebra, 1993), which appears closely related to this question.

I would appreciate references, examples, or characterizations concerning this problem.

Title: Can per-block complementary-slackness residuals localize model-form error to a specific scale in a decomposed multi-scale optimization?
Body:
Body: I'm working with a multi-scale system (biochemical, molecule → cell → tissue → organ → organism → species) decomposed into coupled second-order primal/dual pairs — one pair per scale, with coupling interfaces between adjacent pairs. Each pair carries its own complementary-slackness ("kilter") residual, and the system is solved by sweeping across scales: kilter sweep → basin traversal → parameter update → joint convergence of the duality gap and an inversion residual. What I want: use the per-pair kilter residual as a diagnostic. When the full system fails to predict measurements, I want to say "the break is at the tissue→organ interface" — i.e., localize model-form error to a scale, not just observe global non-convergence. What I've tried: on a 1D higher-order PDE toy (Cahn–Hilliard-type phase field coupled to a reaction–diffusion field), the main configuration reaches a duality gap of ~8e-14 with pair-level residuals ~1e-10, and the per-pair residuals do spike at the pair where I inject model error. But a PDHG configuration on the same problem fails to converge (gap ~27.7), so I can't tell how much of the residual signal means "this scale's model is wrong" versus "the solver is struggling." My questions:

  1. Is there established theory or practice for using per-block KKT/complementary-slackness residuals in decomposed (domain- or scale-decomposed) optimization as a model-error localizer?
  2. Are there known results distinguishing residual patterns caused by model-form error at one block from those caused by solver non-convergence? I've looked at domain-decomposition and multigrid literature, but most of it treats the residual as a solver convergence measure, not as a pointer to which block's model is wrong.

Title: Beyond the least-squares regression line, how can we compute the line that minimizes the sum of any even power of the residuals?
Body:
Given a finite collection of points $\{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i\in I}$ in the plane we can form the least-squares regression line $y = mx+b$ that "best fits" the points by taking the values of $m$ and $b$ that minimize the sum of the squares of the residuals: $\sum_{i\in I} (mx_i+b-y_i)^\mathbf{2}.$ What if instead of the sum of the squares of the residuals, we considered the sum of their fourth powers, or sixth powers, or beyond? (let's not consider odd powers for the sake of avoiding any negativity.) In each of these cases there must be an $m$ and $b$ that minimizes $$\sum_{i\in I} (mx_i+b-y_i)^{2k}\,,$$ so such a line of best fit must exist. For a given power $2k$ can we compute $m$ and $b$ explicitly?

I've started writing out the case for $k=2,$ the fourth powers of the residuals, which, though rather gross, should result in closed-form solutions for $m$ and $b$ since it boils down to determining the root(s) of a cubic. Beyond this case however it would involve higher-degree polynomials, so I see no reason we should expect explicit solutions for $m$ and $b$, … but perhaps this is a skill issue on my part.

Title: When primitive+ irreducible in $A[X]$ implies irreducible in $K[X]$, where $K=\mathrm{Frac}(A)$?
Body:
Let $A$ be a (commutative) domain, with field of fractions $K$.

The following lemma is well-known:

Lemma. Let $f\in A[X]$ be a primitive non constant polynomial. If $f$ is irreducible in $K[X]$, it is also irreducible in $A[X]$.

There are counter-examples to the converse (see below). With some extra assumptions it becomes true (for example, if $A$ is a UFD)

The following proposition is perhaps a litlle less known.

Proposition. Let $A$ be a (commutative) domain, with field of fractions $K$.

The two following properties are equivalent:

(i) Every monic non constant irreducible polynomial in $A[X]$ stays irreducible in $K[X]$

(ii) $A$ is integrally closed (in $K$).

Question. Can we characterize the domains $A$ for which any primitive non constant irreducible polynomial of $A[X]$ stays irreducible in $K[X]$ ?

UFDs are such examples of domains. Are they the only ones ?

Remark. By the proposition, such a domain $A$ is necessarily integrally closed, but this is not enough.

For a counter-example, take $A=\mathbb{Z}[i\sqrt{13}]$ and $f=2X^2+2X+7$, which is primitive irreducible in $A[X]$, but has two roots in $K[X]$ ($A$ is indeed integrally closed because it is the ring of integers of $K$)

Title: Disc (washer) method vs Shell method: any example distinguishing them?
Body:
If a planar region $R$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is revolved around a fixed axis, say $x$-axis, and if the planar region is bounded between $x=a$ and $x=b$, $a<b$, then to compute the volume of the solid of revolution, the commonly used methods are

i) washer (disc) method;

ii) shell method.

In (i), we take slices of the solid by planes perpendicular to the axis of rotation.

In (ii), if I have understood the method correctly, we take cylindrical slices with the line of revolution as the axis of the cylinder; then compute areas of such cylinders, and then sum up (integrate over the levels $x=a$ to $x=b$).

Question 1. Is there any example of any solid object which is a solid of revolution of a planar region, for which one of the methods is applicable, but not the other?

(From the examples illustrated in common books, such as Stewart's or Apostol's Calculus, I saw no such example; it might not exist, but I couldn't justify myself.)

Question 2. Is there any example of any solid object that is a solid of revolution of a planar region, for which it is easier to compute volume by one method than the other?

(Of course, the second question is not precise, since the "easiness" depends on our understanding/maturity in the computations. But, I want an example, in which one method is easy to implement with fewer computations than the other.)

$$ N_p\text{ is a congruent number} \iff p\not\equiv5\pmod 8. $$

Equivalently, for odd primes,

$$ p\equiv1,3,7\pmod 8 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad N_p\text{ is a congruent number}, $$

whereas

$$ p\equiv5\pmod 8 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad N_p\text{ is not a congruent number}. $$

For $p=2$, we have $N_2 = 5$, which is a congruent number.

Since $N_p$ is a congruent number if and only if the elliptic curve

$$ E_{N_p}: y^2=x^3-N_p^2x $$

has positive Mordell--Weil rank, the conjecture is equivalent to

$$ \operatorname{rank}E_{N_p}(\mathbb Q)>0 \iff p\not\equiv5\pmod 8. $$

For odd $p$,

$$ N_p = 2\left(3^{p-1}-3^{p-2}+3^{p-3}-\cdots-3+1\right). $$

Some computed examples are

$$ \begin{array}{c|c|c} p & N_p & \operatorname{rank}E_{N_p}(\mathbb Q)\\ \hline 5 & 122 & 0\\ 13 & 797162 & 0\\ 17 & 64570082 & 0\\ 29 & 34315188682442 & 0\\ 31 & 308836698141974 & 1\\ 37 & 225141952945498682 & 0 \end{array} $$

Can this conjecture be proved using (2)-descent, the Monsky matrix, (2)-Selmer groups, or another method?

In particular, can one prove

$$ p\equiv5\pmod 8 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{rank}E_{N_p}(\mathbb Q)=0, $$

and

$$ p\equiv1,3,7\pmod 8 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{rank}E_{N_p}(\mathbb Q)>0? $$

If the conjecture is false, a counterexample would also be very useful.

Title: How do you explain why the leading coefficient of a quadratic models HALF the acceleration, without referring to calculus?

Title: Laplace transforms: how does the infinite-time limit remain valid in general applications?
Body:
I understand that the Laplace transform is defined by

$$ \mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = \int_0^\infty f(t)e^{-st}\,dt = \lim_{T\to\infty}\int_0^T f(t)e^{-st}\,dt. $$

I also understand that $\infty$ is not a number, and that the infinite integral is defined through this limit.

What I don't understand is what happens afterwards.

For example, we derive

$$ \mathcal{L}\{f'(t)\}=sF(s)-f(0), $$

under suitable conditions. We then use this as a general algebraic rule when solving differential equations and in other applications, without explicitly carrying the $T\to\infty$ limit.

How is the limiting operation in the definition reconciled with this apparently exact, general use of $F(s)$?

In particular, if the physical process being modelled only exists over a finite time, why is a representation based on $t\to\infty$ still an exact representation that can be manipulated independently of that limit?

Title: What is the best way to quantify a performance metric for a game with adaptive difficulty?
Body:
I’m working with a game where, for example, a player has to hit a moving ball with a racket. Every time they successfully hit the ball, the racket becomes smaller, making the next hit progressively more difficult. Once they miss, the racket resets to its original size.

Each round lasts 30 minutes, and I would like to compare performance across rounds.

I also have a chance/control condition where the racket doesn’t move, so some hits can happen simply by chance.

I would like to get a single normalized hit-rate/performance value for each round that tells me whether the player performed well or poorly overall.

Ideally, this value would take into account:

  • The racket getting smaller after each successful hit
  • The racket resetting after a miss
  • The fixed 30-minute duration
  • Different numbers of hits and misses across rounds
  • The chance-level performance from the stationary-racket condition
  • What would be the best way to calculate this as one normalized value?

I’m particularly interested in something that accounts for the increasing difficulty as the racket gets smaller, rather than just calculating hits / total attempts. I have tried to calculate a score using the difference between the actual number of hits and the expected value of hits, but I think it does not take into account the paddle starting from where they last hit the ball (if it did not miss).

Also, if anyone knows of similar studies or experiments that have used a comparable normalized performance/hit-rate metric, I’d really appreciate any references or examples.

Title: Is a pull-back a contravariant functor?
Body:
I am reading through "Analysis, Manifolds and Physics", and I've gotten to page 116 where pullbacks are introduced for differentiable manifolds. They introduce the idea of the pull back of a mapping $g$ under $f$, as $f^*g=g\circ f$, and then they say we have here an example of a contravariant functor. Specifically, if $X,Y,Z$ are differentiable manifolds, $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to Z$ are differentiable mappings, $E,F,G$ are vector spaces of functions defined on $X,Y,Z$ and:$$\begin{align} C(X)&=E\quad C(Y)=F\quad C(Z)=G \\ C(f)&=f^*:F\to E\quad \text{by} \quad f^*h=h\circ f \\ C(g)&=g^*:G\to F\quad \text{by} \quad g^*k=k\circ g \end{align}$$

Then C is a contravariant functor: $$(g\circ f)^*:G\to E\quad \text{by} \quad (g\circ f)^*k=k\circ g\circ f$$.

I am confused by what exactly is being done here. It doesn't specify what $h$ and $k$ are, so I am unsure whether they are functions on the Manifolds (and if so what their codomain is ), or mappings between them. I am also unsure what $C$ is and what it does to the manifolds, and why it acts on the way it does on the mappings $f,g$. Finally, I don't get how the final result shows that $C$ is a contravariant functor, since my understanding is a contravariant functor should reverse the order of composition. Any clarification would be welcome.

Title: Prime test for Proth Numbers - generalised - is it valid?

The essence of the generalisation is replacing the section below

$p > 2^{k+2}. N < 2^{2k+3}$ with a form that includes integer variable j (j>=3) as follows

$p > 2^{k+(j-1)}. N < 2^{2k+j}$

The generalisation will apply to all numbers of the form $(2^k-1)\cdot2^{k+j}+1$ ( where j is a positive integer >= 3)

Alternative generalisations may be accepted.

The j=4 case in particular is asked for in question 5151872

Generalising this proof to more families provides many more areas for prime searching as $(2^k-1)\cdot2^{k+j}+1$ is an infinite number of sets.

Note: Beyond j=4 the converse is problematic

The key property we would have to rely upon to prove the converse is perhaps Gauss theorem on bi-quadratic reciprocity.

For some sets of numbers it is possible to show N cannot be expressed as $a^2 + 64{c}^2$, for others this is a problem.

Only for j=3 and j=4 might we consider this test a deterministic test (based on current analysis)

Title: What's so special about the Lebesgue measure (for $\mathbb{R}^n$)?
Body:
Let $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ denote the set of Lebesgue-measurable subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\mu$ denote the Lebesgue measure. Regarding measures for $\mathbb{R^n}$, it seems that it is possible to extend the Lebesgue measure to some larger $\sigma$-algebra $\mathscr{F}$ (i.e. $\mathscr{F} \supsetneq \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$) such that for the extended measure $\nu$ on $\mathscr{F}$, $S \in \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) \implies \nu(S) = \mu(S)$. This raises the question of why Lebesgue measure is so commonly used, rather than some such extended measure that works for more subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

My tentative understanding is that it's because the Lebesgue measure has the desirable properties of being both countably additive and translation-invariant, but any extension of the Lebesgue measure of the kind just described cannot have both these properties.

It this correct? Or is the preference for Lebesgue measure due to some other desirable properties that such extensions don't have (e.g. rotation-invariance)? Or just for the utilitarian reason that Lebesgue measure works for most subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ of practical interest?

Title: Can the Euler integral for the Gamma function be derived naturally from its recurrence relation and operator structure?
Body:
I am a beginner in mathematics, so some of my understanding of the concepts may be incomplete or inaccurate.

I am trying to understand whether the Gamma function can be obtained by treating its recurrence relation as a linear-algebraic problem.

Starting from

$$ \Gamma(x+1)=x\Gamma(x), $$

I tried to regard this as an operator equation. I defined

$$ (Tf)(x)=f(x+1) $$

as the translation operator, and

$$ (Mf)(x)=xf(x) $$

as the multiplication operator. The recurrence then becomes

$$ T\Gamma=M\Gamma. $$

I also found that these two operators satisfy

$$ (TM-MT)f=f(x+1)=Tf, $$

so that

$$ [T,M]=T. $$

My idea was to treat this as an operator equation and try to solve it directly in order to obtain the Gamma function.

Since (T) is a translation operator, I then tried Fourier analysis. Under the Fourier transform, the translation operator becomes multiplication by (e$^{it}$), while the multiplication operator (M) becomes a differentiation operator. This turns the operator equation into

$$ iG'(t)=e^{it}G(t), $$

whose solution is

$$ G(t)=Ce^{-e^{it}}. $$

However, this does not seem to lead naturally to the usual Euler integral representation

$$ \Gamma(x)=\int_0^\infty t^{x-1}e^{-t}\,dt. $$

So this approach seems to have failed, at least for the goal I had in mind.

What I would like to understand is whether there is a more natural way to formulate this as an operator or linear-algebra problem that actually leads to the Euler integral.

In particular, I would like to understand where the kernel

$$ t^{x-1} $$

comes from, rather than simply assuming it and then verifying that the resulting integral satisfies the recurrence relation.

I suspect that the Mellin transform may be the appropriate tool here, but I do not yet see how it arises naturally from the operator equation above.

Title: What is the probability that a random Rubik's Cube will have four faces with the exact same raw count of colors, regardless of their grid positions?
Body:
I am trying to calculate the probability that a randomly scrambled Rubik's Cube will have at least four faces with the exact same raw count of colors, regardless of their grid positions.

Some information that might be helpful:

Let $v_c$ be the number of stickers of color $c$ on a given face. Since there are only 9 total stickers of any single color on the entire cube, if $k$ faces have an identical tally vector $V = (v_1, \dots, v_6)$, the total stickers across those faces must satisfy: $$k \cdot v_c \leq 9 \implies v_c \leq \left\lfloor \frac{9}{k} \right\rfloor$$

For $k = 4$, the constraint $4v_c \leq 9$ implies $v_c \in \{0, 1, 2\}$. Solving $\sum_{c=1}^6 v_c = 9$ leaves only two integer partitions for the matching faces' color distributions:

$(2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1)$ — Three colors appear twice, three appear once.

$(2, 2, 2, 2, 1, 0)$ — Four colors appear twice, one appears once, one is absent. Due to fixed center facets, the color with count 0 cannot be any of the four chosen faces' center colors.

Title: Formal mapping between infinite branch cuts and finite singularities in improper evaluations
Body:
I am analyzing the topological equivalence between an infinite branch cut and a finite singularity using a specific improper evaluation.

Consider the integral: $$ \int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{x\sqrt{x^{2}-1}}dx $$

Evaluating this natively in the complex plane requires a contour around the branch cut between $z = -1$ and $z = 1$.

However, applying the projective geometry inversion $x = \frac{1}{u}$ maps the point at infinity directly to the origin, transforming the evaluation to a finite asymptote: $$ \int_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}du = \frac{\pi}{2} $$

Furthermore, evaluating the limit of the complex logarithmic definition of the boundary as $x \to \infty$ yields a collapse via $i \cdot i = -1$: $$ \lim_{x\rightarrow\infty} \left[ -i \ln\left(\frac{1}{x}+i\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{x^{2}}}\right) \right] = -i\left(i\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = \frac{\pi}{2} $$

Questions:

  1. Does this specific projective inversion ($x = 1/u$) rigorously prove that the infinite branch cut contour is topologically identical to the finite singularity evaluation without any hidden branch-cut obstructions?
  2. In established complex geometry literature, is there a formalized theorem that classifies this exact mapping where these distinct topologies collapse into the identical logarithmic limit?

Title: Every even perfect number proper divisor Congruent Number
Body:
Every even perfect number $N>6$ has the form

$$ N=2^{p-1}(2^p-1), $$

where $p$ and $2^p-1$ are prime.

I call a proper divisor $d$ of $N$ a Congruent Number if

$$ d>\sqrt N. $$

Conjecture: For every even perfect number $N>6$, the number of Congruent Numbers is

$$ 2k,\qquad k>0. $$

For example:

$$ 28:\quad 7,14 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 2k=2,\ k=1. $$

$$ 496:\quad 31,62,124,248 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 2k=4,\ k=2. $$

Therefore, the total number of Congruent Numbers among those proper divisors is $2k$.

Question: Is this conjecture true for every even perfect number $N>6$? If so, can it be proved?

Title: $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} (-1)^{n+1} (3n+1)^{-s} = 0 $ implies $Re(s) < \frac{\ln(2)}{3} + \frac{\pi}{3 \sqrt 3}$?
Body:
Consider the Dirichlet series

$$f(s) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} (-1)^{n+1} (3n+1)^{-s}$$

We know

$$f(1) = \frac{\ln(2)}{3} + \frac{\pi}{3 \sqrt 3}$$

And I wonder if

$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} (-1)^{n+1} (3n+1)^{-s} = 0 $ implies $Re(s) < \frac{\ln(2)}{3} + \frac{\pi}{3 \sqrt 3}$ ?

I looked for counterexamples but I could not find any. I computed the first few zero's but found nothing close to this boundary.

By some kind of analogue

It is well known but not proven that

$$\zeta(s,+1) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^{-s}$$

$$\zeta(s,-1) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (-1)^{n+1}n^{-s}$$

$$\zeta(s,+2) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} (2n+1)^{-s}$$

$$\zeta(s,-2) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} (-1)^{n+1}(2n+1)^{-s}$$

have all of their nonreal zero's on the line $Re(s) = 1/2$.

These are the famous Riemann zeta, Eta and Dirichlet Beta functions.

Notice how $Re(s) = 1/2 < g(1)$ where $g(1)$ is the function value at $1$ for these.

So it seems a universal thing at first.

It seems we can generalize it. Although these small cases ofcourse are too little to speak of a trend.

But for now just analyse the $f(s)$ given above as a test case.

Notice $f(s)$ unlike the others, does not an euler product and no critical line. But the inequality with $f(1)$ might still hold.

Title: A description of the Besov space $B_{\infty, \infty}^0$

Title: Assigning Vectors to Graph Nodes with Edge-Specific Vector Spaces and Path Decomposition Constraints
Body:
Let ${G}=({V},{E})$ be a connected undirected graph. The node and edge sets of ${G}$ are denoted by ${V}=\left\{ 1,2,\ldots,n\right\} $ and ${E}\subseteq{V}\times{V}$, respectively. For each edge $(i,j)\in{E}$, let $\varOmega_{ij}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}$ be a linear vector space associated with the edge $(i,j)$. Let ${P}_{ij}$ be the set of all paths from node $i$ to node $j$ excluding the direct edge $(i,j)$. For any vector $\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\varOmega_{ij}$ and any path $p\in{P}_{ij}$ consisting of edges $(v_{0},v_{1}),(v_{1},v_{2}),\dots,(v_{k-1},v_{k})$ (where $v_{0}=i,v_{k}=j)$, there exists a decomposition $\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{1}+\cdots+\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{k}$ along with $p$ such that $\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{l}\in\varOmega_{v_{l-1},v_{l}}$, where $l\in\left\{ 1,2,\cdots,k\right\} $ and $\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{l}$ can be equal to $\boldsymbol{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$.

Is it possible to assign a vector $\boldsymbol{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ to each node where $i\in1,2,\cdots,n$ such that for every edge $(i,j)\in{E}$, the vector difference satisfies $\boldsymbol{x}_{i}-\boldsymbol{x}_{j}\in\varOmega_{ij}$ and there exist at least two nodes $u,v\in{V}$ such that $\boldsymbol{x}_{u}\neq\boldsymbol{x}_{v}$？

Title: Triangular Numbers $T_i$ Dividing Consecutive-Integer Concatenations $N_i,$ e.g. $T_5\mid N_5$ i.e. $\frac{5\cdot 6}2\mid 12345$
Body:
Let $N_n$ be the positive integer obtained by concatenating the integers $(1,2,\dots,n)$ in their usual decimal representation.

Thus,

$$ N_1=1, \qquad N_2=12, \qquad N_3=123, \qquad N_4=1234, $$

and, for example,

$$ N_{12}=123456789101112. $$

Let

$$ T_n=1+2+\cdots+n=\frac{n(n+1)}{2} $$

be the n-th triangular number.

I want to determine all positive integers $n$ for which the concatenated number $N_n$ is divisible by its triangular number $T_n$; that is,

$$ T_n\mid N_n. $$

Equivalently, we want

$$ \frac{N_n}{T_n} = \frac{2N_n}{n(n+1)} $$

to be an integer.

For the first few values we obtain

$$ \frac{N_1}{T_1} = \frac{1}{1} =1, $$

$$ \frac{N_2}{T_2} = \frac{12}{3} =4, $$

and

$$ \frac{N_5}{T_5} = \frac{12345}{15} =823. $$

Thus

$$ n=1,\;2,\;5 $$

are solutions.

This problem is listed in OEIS as A072725, where the corresponding quotients are

$$ 1,\;4,\;823. $$

The OEIS entry also mentions that a probability argument suggests that the sequence may be finite.

My question is:

Are

$$ \boxed{n=1,2,5} $$

the only positive integers satisfying

$$ \boxed{\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\mid N_n}? $$

If so, is there a proof that no further solutions exist?

If not, what is the next value of (n)?

Title: How long (in real time) would the proposed singularities in the Euler and Navier-Stokes equations take to occur?
Body:
Buckmaster and Alpöge and OpenAI have recently claimed to give examples of smooth initial conditions that lead to finite-time singularities under time evolution given by the Euler equations and by the Navier-Stokes equations, respectively.

Obviously these solutions are highly idealized, and in reality, new physics would kick multiple times at different scales if we tried to actually engineer those setups. But what if we ignore all those physical details and just naively reverse the nondimensionalization by plugging in macroscopic parameters for, say, water at room temperature? How much "wall-clock" time would it take for the singularity to appear in each case?

Obviously there is some arbitrariness to the answer, depending on when we choose to "start the clock". Relatedly, I assume that there are probably a few different free parameters in the nondimensionalization, e.g. a length scale for the variation in the initial conditions, and maybe a velocity scale for the initial conditions as well (since the incompressible Euler and N-S equations don't include a finite speed of sound to set a reference scale for velocity). So the final answer probably won't be a single time duration, but some simple power-law function of those free parameters. What is that function? (The general form of that function probably comes from the standard nondimensionalization in the setup of the problem, but the numerical constant coefficient presumably depends on the specific newly proposed solutions.)

Title: Is there a textbook on first order logic which satisfies my requirements?
Body:
Does a textbook on first-order logic exist which satisfies these three criteria:

  1. Notation: Given a function symbol $f$ in the language $\mathcal{L}$ and variables $x, y, \cdots$, the corresponding term is written as $f(x, y, \cdots)$ and not $fxy\cdots$. Plus, the binary connectives are always written in infix notation i.e. $\phi \wedge \psi$ and not $\wedge \phi \psi$.
  2. Proof System: The proof system is non-axiomatic and only has rules of inference. Plus, any proof is written in a linear sequence (so not as a tree) as \begin{align} 1. \quad \Gamma_1 &\vdash \phi_1 \qquad \text{(Rule of inference used)} \\ 2. \quad \Gamma_2 &\vdash \phi_2 \qquad \text{(Rule of inference used)} \\ &\ \vdots \end{align}
  3. Soundness and Completeness Theorem: The book contains a proof of the soundness and completeness theorems for 1st order logic for all formulae, not just sentences.

I've been searching for days now and have not been able to find any books which satisfy these criteria. The closest was Hedman's A First Course in Logic, but it proves the completeness theorem only for sentences.

If there are multiple books which satisfy these three criteria, I would appreciate it if any answers would specify whether the books also satisfy some additional criteria, arranged in decreasing order of importance:

  1. The book discusses propositional logic first, establishing a proof system for it and proving the soundness and completeness theorems for it, before moving on to 1st order logic.
  2. The book proves Godel's two incompleteness theorems.
  3. The book proves Lindstrom's theorem.

None of these additional criteria are dealbreakers. Rather, they're just things I would like to have in a book.

Any help in providing such textbooks will be much appreciated.

Title: "Smallest" choice principle that's equivalent to $\mathsf{AC}$?

My question is: Is there a smallest (ordered by $\subset$) class $C$ where $\mathsf{ZF+AC}_C \implies \mathsf{ZFC}$? An easy starting point is $\mathsf{AC}=\mathsf{AC}_V$ of course, but we could remove $V_\omega$ (giving $\mathsf{AC}_{V-V_\omega}$), as each hereditary finite set has a choice function (I believe). Title: Citation for Clenshaw-Curtis weights precomputation by DCT on Wikipedia?
Body:
I'm struggling to find a citation for the elegantly simple algorithm for precomputation of quadrature weights for Clenshaw-Curtis quadrature by DCT that is given on the Wikipedia page https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clenshaw%E2%80%93Curtis_quadrature#Precomputing_the_quadrature_weights.

I've looked at:

  • The original Clenshaw&Curtis (1960) - does not use FFT/DCT
  • Gentleman (1972) uses DCT to calcuate an integral, but does not calcutate the quadrature weights.
  • Waldvogel (2006) uses FFT to calculate the quadrature weights, but the algorithm does not look the same as the Wikipedia page (I must be missing something? I don't understand how there can be two different DCT/FFT methods to get the same weights) and appears significantly more convoluted.
  • Sommariva (2013) uses a DCT approach, but for general weight functions (I only care about the standard $w(x)=1$ weight function), and I do not see a method as simple as the Wikipedia one.
  • Boyd's textbook "Chebyshev and Fourier spectral methods" p. 456 gives a summation formula for the quadrature weights, but not a DCT/FFT method
  • Just to note @dharr's comment - the Wikipedia page cites Imhof (1963), but the citation only refers to the statement "The weights $w_{n}$ are positive and their sum is equal to one." Imhof does not address the calculation of quadrature weights.

Title: Partial sums in Newton's binomial formula
Body:
Let $\alpha,A$ be real numbers such that $0<\alpha<1$, $A>0$. Let $n,k$ be positive integers. Then $$1=(\alpha+(1-\alpha))^{n+k}=\sum_{i=0}^{n+k}\binom{n+k}{i} (1-\alpha)^i\alpha^{n+k-i}.$$ Now consider the partial sum $$P_{n,k}=\sum_{i=0}^{k}\binom{n+k}{i} (1-\alpha)^i\alpha^{n+k-i}.$$

This formula relates to probability theory and computer science. A few years ago, to secure data storage, it was proposed to construct $n+k$ files ($k>0$) from $n$ files of roughly equal size, such that from any $n$ chosen from the $n+k$, the original $n$ files could be reconstructed. For example this could be done by using a $n\times(n+k)$ integer matrix such that all $n\times n$ minors ar invertible.

If $\alpha$ is the probability that one file is not corrupted, then $\alpha^n$ is the probability that no file in the original ones is corrupted.

In the case of the $n+k$ files, if I made no error, $P_{n,k}$ is the probability that we can recover the $n$ first files from the $n+k$ new.

I suppose that $k$ is proportional to $n$ ($k=[An]$). I would like to know $$\lim_{n\to\infty}P_{n,[An]} .$$

Title: What is the topological argument principle and how does it relate to proper maps between topological discs?
Body:

I quote:

$K$ is a topological disc, and on any sequence of points $\{p_j\}$ that converges to its boundary, $\partial K$, the image sequence $\{\phi(p_j)\}$ converges to $\partial \mathbb{D}$. Thus $\phi: K\to \bar{\mathbb{D}}$ is what is known as a proper map. Putting its properties together, $\phi$ is a proper, continuous, and locally one-to-one map between topological discs. By the topological argument principle, $\phi$ is globally one-to-one.

Is there any heuristic that could help me see why global injectivity follows from the conditions on $\phi$? Or is there a reference that explains the "topological version" of the complex-analytic argument principle?

Title: Conjecture: For integer $N\geq2$, there is at least one integer $C$, with $N^2<C<(N+1)^2$, that is the area of a right triangle with rational sides
Body:
I have the following conjecture:

Conjecture. For every integer $N \ge 2$, there exists at least one congruent number $C$ such that

$$N^2 < C < (N+1)^2.$$

Recall that a positive integer $C$ is called a congruent number if it is the area of a right triangle whose three side lengths are rational numbers.

For example:

  • For $N=2$, the interval is $(4,9)$, and $5,6,7$ are congruent numbers.
  • For $N=3$, the interval is $(9,16)$, and $13,14,15$ are congruent numbers.
  • For $N=4$, the interval is $(16,25)$, and $20,21,24$ are congruent numbers.

Thus, the conjecture holds for these small values of $N$.

My question is:

Is this conjecture true for every integer $N \ge 2$?

If the conjecture is known, I would like to know whether there is a proof or a counterexample. If it is currently open, I would be interested in any known results concerning the existence of congruent numbers in intervals between consecutive squares.

I would also be interested in possible connections with the elliptic curves

$$ E_C:\quad y^2=x^3-C^2x, $$

which are associated with the Congruent Number Problem (determining when a number is congruent).

Title: Max/Min of $|z|$, if $|z^2+z-1|=2$
Body:
Given that $$|z^2+z-1|=2\tag{$\ast$}$$ $$\implies 2=|z^2+z-1|=|(z+1/2)^2-5/4|\ge ||z+1/2|^2-5/4|$$ $$\implies ||z+1/2|^2-5/4|\le 2\implies |z+1/2|\le \frac{\sqrt{13}}{2}$$ Next, we write $$\frac{\sqrt{13}}{2}\ge |z+1/2| \ge ||z|-1/2| \implies |z|\le \frac{1+\sqrt{13}}{2}$$ So, we get $|z|_{\max.}=\frac{1+\sqrt{13}}{2}$.

Notice that $$z=\omega=\frac{-1+i\sqrt{3}}{2}$$ satisfies $(*)$, giving us $|z|=1$.

A plot of $(*)$ in Argand plane shows that it is a closed figure indicating that $|z|_{\min.}=1$.

The question is: How to get $|z|_{\min.}$ for $(*)$, and is it really $1$?
