There is a relation with the Fox H-function, given by $$ V_{p,q}^{\alpha,\beta} \left[ \left. \begin{matrix} (\mathbf{a}_p,\mathbf{A}_p)\\ (\mathbf{b}_q,\mathbf{B}_q) \end{matrix} \right| x \right] = \int_0^\rho H_{q,p}^{p,0} \left( t \left| \begin{matrix} (\mathbf{b}_q,\mathbf{B}_q)\\ (\mathbf{a}_p,\mathbf{A}_p) \end{matrix} \right. \right) \frac{x^\alpha\,\mathrm dt} {t\,\log^{\beta+1}(1/(tx))}. $$

The H-function has a natural computable representation (infinity series), I was wondering if this Volterra function also have some series representation. I’d appreciate any ideas, thanks in advance.

Title: Diagonal action of $C_2$ on product of spheres

Title: Doubt about sheaf condition in Ben Williams notes

Title: Orders of outer automorphisms of $S_6$
Body:
It is known that the only symmetric group $S_n$ that has an outer automorphism is the case where $n=6$.

The order of a permutation in $S_6$ (and hence also of its corresponding inner automorphism) is given by the lcm of its disjoint cycle lengths. Hence, the order may be $1, 2, 3, 4, 5,$ or $6$.

If $f$ is an outer automorphism of $S_6$, then $f^2$ is an inner automorphism (because the outer automorphism group of $S_6$ is cyclic of order $2$), hence the order of $f^2$ must be $1, 2, 3, 4, 5,$ or $6$. Also, the order of $f$ must be even for the same reason, hence it must be twice the order of $f^2$. This means that the order of $f$ must be $2, 4, 6, 8, 10,$ or $12$.

But do all six potential orders of outer automorphisms of $S_6$ actually occur? The order $2$ case is known to be possible (see An Example of Outer Automorphism of $S_6$ with order 2?), so it remains to check the other five potential orders.

Title: Monotonicity of $\vert{}\zeta(z)\vert{}$ along the semicircular path $z = 1 - 5e^{iu}$

Numerical evaluations strongly suggest that the modulus $\vert{}\zeta(z(u))\vert{}$ is strictly increasing with respect to $u$ on the interval $[0, \pi]$. Consequently, the global maximum of the modulus along this path is achieved at $u = \pi$, giving a maximum value of $\zeta(6)$.

I have considered using the functional equation to map the behavior back to the right half-plane, but managing the modulus of the gamma factor and the sine factor along a circular arc becomes highly non-trivial.

Is there a standard technique or an elegant way to analytically prove this strict monotonicity without relying heavily on computer-assisted interval arithmetic? Is a proof using computed-assisted interval arithmetic considered to be "correct"?

Hence, $$\begin{aligned} 1 - 1 + 1 - 1 + 1 - 1 \dots &= \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{1-r} \quad \text{when } r = -1 \\ 1 - 2 + 3 - 4 + 5 - 6 \dots &= \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{(1-r)^2} \quad \text{when } r = -1 \\ 1 - 3 + 6 - 10 + 15 \dots &= \frac{1}{8} = \frac{1}{(1-r)^3} \quad \text{when } r = -1 \end{aligned}$$

Title: Is there any function you can integrate with respect to $\sqrt{dx}$ (using my definition of what that would mean) and get a finite nonzero result?
Body:
Messing around trying to build intuition for manipulating differentials, I had the idea to try and raise them to powers in a single integral expression.

Using this specific definition of definite integration from 0 to 1:

$$\int_0^1f(x)dx=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}{f\left({i\over n}\right)n^{-1}}$$

My understanding is that $dx$ represents the $n^{-1}$ term, which should means that if a similar single integral expression with a squared differential were to mean anything, it would be: $$\int_0^1f(x)(dx)^2=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f\left({i\over n}\right)\left(n^{-1}\right)^2$$

A geometric intuition for this is: rather than the limit of rectangles of decreasing base size touching $f(x)$ in their top left corner, the expression is instead counting the volume of boxes built by extending each of those rectangles into the z-axis by its base length.

For a typical function, like a polynomial or exponential, this will always evaluate to zero. However, you plug the function $g(x)={{1}\over(x-1)^2}$ into the squared-differential-integral, the pole grows at the same rate the $n^{-2}$ term shrinks, and you get $$\int_0^1g(x)(dx)^2 = \lim_{n\to\infty} \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \left({1\over {\left({i\over n}-1\right)^2}}\left(n^{-1}\right)^2\right)= \lim_{n\to\infty} \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} {1\over {\left(i-n\right)^2}}= \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} {1\over m^2}= {\pi^2\over 6} $$

I tried to find a similar function where you can take a definite integral with $\sqrt{dx}$, but $h(x)=\sqrt{x\over {x-1}}$ seems to make the whole thing blow up to infinity. Is there any function where the expression below is finite and nonzero? $$\lim_{n \to \infty}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}{h\left({i\over n}\right)\over \sqrt{n}}$$

Title: Example of ring where $n\cdot a\neq na$
Body:
In Gallian's Contemporary Abstract Algebra he gives the following sidenote when defining rings that had me scratching my head for why such a note would be necessary.

Recall that if $a$ is an element from a group under the operation of addition and $n$ is a positive integer, $na$ means $a+a+\ldots+a$, where there are $n$ summands. When dealing with rings, this notation can cause confusion, since we also use juxtaposition for the ring multiplication. When there is the potential for confusion, we will use $n\cdot a$ to mean $a+a+\ldots+a$ ($n$ summands).

I cannot think of an example where such confusion would happen, and as far as I can tell, Gallian never brings up an example where he needs to appeal to this convention for distinguishing $na$ and $n\cdot a$. If we consider an example like a matrix ring, $nA=\underbrace{A+\ldots+A}_{n-\text{times}}$, and $nA$ here does not denote ring multiplication. However, no ambiguity arises in whether we mean ring multiplication or repeated summation since $n$ is clearly not an element of the ring (and thus not a candidate for ring multiplication).

Can anyone think of an example that has "the potential for confusion?"

Title: Bolzano-Weierstrass Theorem in $(\mathbb{R}^m,d_2)$
Body:
I want to prove the following statement:

If $(x_n)$ is a bounded sequence in $(\mathbb{R}^m,d_2)$, then $(x_n)$ has a convergent subsequence in $(\mathbb{R}^m,d_2)$.

My attempt:

Let $(x_n)$ be a bounded sequence in $(\mathbb{R}^m,d_2)$. Write

$$ x_n=(x_n^{(1)},x_n^{(2)},\ldots,x_n^{(m)}). $$

Since $(x_n)$ is bounded, there exists $M>0$ such that

$$ d_2(x_n,0)\leq M $$

for every $n$. Hence,

$$ \sqrt{(x_n^{(1)})^2+\cdots+(x_n^{(m)})^2}\leq M, $$

and therefore

$$ |x_n^{(i)}|\leq M $$

for each $i=1,\ldots,m$.

Thus, each coordinate sequence $(x_n^{(i)})$ is bounded in $\mathbb{R}$. By the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem, $(x_n^{(1)})$ has a convergent subsequence.

From this subsequence, I take a further subsequence for which $(x_n^{(2)})$ converges. Continuing this process for all $m$ coordinates, since $m$ is finite, I obtain a subsequence $(x_{n_k})$ such that

$$ x_{n_k}^{(i)}\to a_i $$

for every $i=1,\ldots,m.$

Let

$$ a=(a_1,\ldots,a_m). $$

I am not sure how to rigorously prove from here that

$$ d_2(x_{n_k},a)\to 0. $$

I would appreciate any suggestions for completing my proof.

Title: Die with prime number of faces implies events are not independent why?
Body:
I am studying Probability: an Introduction by Grimmett and Welsh (1986).

Exercise 25 in section 1.7 of chapter 1 is as follows:

On your desk there is a very special die which has a prime number $p$ of faces, and you throw this die once. Show that no two events $A$ and $B$ can be independent unless either $A$ or $B$ is the whole sample space or the empty set.

If the die is a fair one, the exercise is trivially simple: you use $\Pr(A) \Pr(B) = \Pr(A \cap B)$ iff $A$ and $B$ are independent, and note that $|A \cap B|$ would then need to be divisible by $p^2$ etc. etc.

But if the die is not fair (and G&W do not assert that fact), it's not so easy.

By using $\Pr(A) = \Pr(A \cap B) + \Pr (A \setminus B)$ I arrive eventually at the quadratic:

$$w^2 + w (u + v - 1) + u v = 0$$

where $u = \Pr(A \setminus B), v = \Pr(B \setminus A), w = \Pr(A \cap B)$.

This leads to:

$$w = \dfrac {1 - u - v = \sqrt {(1 - u - v)^2 - 4 u v} } 2$$

At this stage I'm lost in the thicket of inequalities, where I presume I would need to prove that $(1 - u - v)^2 < 4 u v$ unless those conditions stated above hold.

And as for why $p$ needs to be prime for the above to hold, I am all at sea, and so I believe the intended audience would be; it is aimed at 1st year undergrads, and exercises are described as being "mostly routine".

Is it a reasonable assumption to suppose that Grimmett and Welsh mistakenly omitted to state that the die in question is actually fair?

Title: Closed-form solutions for two families of Infinitely nested radicals (INR)
Body:
Let $(f_n)_{n\ge1}$ be a given sequence of positive integers. For example, $f_n=\frac{n^2+n}{2}$ gives the sequence of triangular numbers (OEIS A000217). For $N\ge1$, define $$A_N(f)=f_1+\sqrt{f_2+\sqrt{f_3+\sqrt{\cdots+\sqrt{f_N}}}}, \quad M_N(f)=f_1\sqrt{f_2\sqrt{f_3\sqrt{\cdots\sqrt{f_N}}}}$$

If the limits exist, let $\displaystyle \operatorname{AINR}(f)=\lim_{N\to\infty}A_N(f)$ and $\displaystyle \operatorname{MINR}(f)=\lim_{N\to\infty}M_N(f)$. For the constant sequence $f_n=12$, we have $\operatorname{AINR}(f)=12+\sqrt{12+\sqrt{12+\cdots}}=16$. For $f_n=n$, the value $\operatorname{MINR}(f)=1\cdot\sqrt{2\cdot\sqrt{3\cdot\sqrt{4\cdots}}}$ is the square of the number known as the Somos quadratic recurrence constant. Are there other known sequences $(f_n)$ for which $\operatorname{AINR}(f)$ or $\operatorname{MINR}(f)$ has a closed form? Here, “closed form” means an expression involving standard functions and named constants such as $\pi$, $e$, Euler’s constant $\gamma$, $\cos$, or the gamma function $\Gamma$

Title: Combinatorics task about cycles
Body:
Initially, problrem arose in computational geometry - I am exploring space-filled curves, through the triangulation of plane and sphere. But I have formulated the question entirely in combinatorics terms.

Let us have $N$ triples, composed of (different) natural numbers:
$$t_i = \{t_{i,1}, t_{i,2}, t_{i,3}\}, t_{i,j} \in \mathbb{N}$$ and the already constructed "hamiltonian cycle": $$t_1 \to t_2 \to \dots \to t_N \to t_1$$

such that neighboring triples necessarily have exactly two common elements:

$$\lvert t_i \cap t_{i+1} \rvert = 2$$ (meaning the adjoining triangles by common edge).

Here and below: $$\langle i\rangle_N = ((i-1)\bmod N)+1 \\ t_{i\pm k}:=t_{\langle i\pm k\rangle_N} $$

For example (cycle through tetrahedron faces):

$$\{1, 2, 4\} \to \{1, 4, 3\} \to \{1, 3, 2\} \to \{2, 3, 4\} \to \{1, 2, 4\}$$

We need to build a more rigorous cycle:

$$t'_1 \to t'_2 \to \dots \to t'_N \to t'_1$$ such that the last element of each triple is the same as the first element of the next:

$$t'_{i, 3} = t'_{i+1, 1}$$

while:

  • $t'_i$ is some permutation of $t_i$
  • The order of triples in the cycle does not change

For the above example:

$$\{2, 1, 4\} \to \{4, 3, 1\} \to \{1, 2, 3\} \to \{3, 4, 2\} \to \{2, 1, 4\}$$

Using the method of trial and error, I was able to formulate the following algorithm for obtaining rigorous cycle:
$$t'_{i,1} = t_{i-2} \cap t_{i-1} \cap t_i\\ t'_{i,2} = t_{i+2} \cap t_{i+1} \cap t_i\\ t'_{i,3} = t_{i-1} \cap t_{i+1} \cap t_i \\$$

Although for all the tested examples it works, I don’t really understand how, and not sure that it will always yield results. Perhaps the whole problem can be formalized differently. For example, using graph theory (or even using hypergraphs). And obtain the required cycle in a more natural and provable way.

Title: Divergence of double sequence $a_{mn} = \frac{m \cdot n}{m^2 + n^2}$
Body:
I'm trying to prove that double sequence $a_{mn} = \frac{m \cdot n}{m^2 + n^2}$ diverges. I.e., that $\lim_{m,n \to \infty}{a_{mn}}$ does not exist.

Does the following approach make sense?

(The proof presented in the solutions manual for Exercise 2.3.13 b) in "Stephen Abbott - Understanding Analysis 2nd edition" introduces a Lemma to prove the fact and is more complex so I thought that I might have overlooked something.)

Proof by contradiction

Assume that $\lim_{m,n \to \infty}{a_{mn}} = A$ for some $A \in \mathbb{R}$. Then for a given $\epsilon > 0$ we can find an $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $m,n \ge N$ it holds that $\left|a_{mn} - A\right| < \epsilon$.

Now let $m = N$ and $n = 2N$. Then $$\epsilon > \left|a_{mn} - A\right| = \left|\frac{2N^2}{5N^2} - A\right| = \left|\frac{2}{5} - A\right|.$$ If we let $m = N$ and $n = 3N$, then $$\epsilon > \left|a_{mn} - A\right| = \left|\frac{3N^2}{10N^2} - A\right| = \left|\frac{3}{10} - A\right|.$$ When adding the inequalities we get $$\left|\frac{2}{5} - A\right| + \left|\frac{3}{10} -A\right| < 2\epsilon.$$ Application of the triangle inequality yields $$\left|\frac{2}{5} - \frac{3}{10}\right| \le \left|\frac{2}{5} - A\right| + \left|A - \frac{3}{10}\right| < 2\epsilon.$$ And thus $\frac{1}{20} < \epsilon$. Since $\epsilon > 0$ is chosen arbitrarily, this is a contradiction and therefore $\lim_{m,n \to \infty}{a_{mn}}$ does not exist.

Title: Triangle inequality for distance between points and subset of a metric space
Body:
I wish to prove that if $(X,d)$ is a metric space, and $A \subseteq X$ is nonempty, then for points $x,y\in X$, we have $D(x,A)\leq d(x,y)+ D(y,A)$, where $$D(x,A) = \inf\{d(x,a)\mid a \in A\}$$ and similarly for $D(y,A)$.

We have

$$d(x,a) \leq d(x,y) + d(y,a)\tag{1}\label{1}$$

for any particular $a$, from the triangle inequality of the original metric space. We now take the inf over $a\in A$ for the left side, which gives us

$$D(x,A) \leq d(x,y) + d(y,a)\tag{2}\label{2}.$$

I attempted now to complete the proof by taking the inf on the right side of $\eqref{1}$ as well, but doubt this is legitimate since $\eqref{1}$ only applied to a given particular $a$, which is then inherited by $\eqref{2}$ from $\eqref{1}$.

Title: A question about the columns in the triangle of Stirling numbers of the first kind
Body:
It is known that the rows of both Stirling number triangles (first kind ${n \brack k}$ and second kind ${n \brace k}$) are log-concave sequences. This is also true for the main diagonals in the triangles: for fixed $k$ and for all $n$ larger than $k$, we have $$ {n \brack n-k}^2\ge {n+1 \brack n+1-k}{n-1 \brack n-1-k} $$ and $${n \brace n-k}^2\ge {n+1 \brace n+1-k}{n-1 \brace n-1-k}. $$ Along the columns, the situation is slightly different: log-concavity holds only for the Stirling numbers of the second kind: for fixed $k$ and for all $ n> k$, we have $${n \brace k}^2\ge {n+1 \brace k}{n-1 \brace k}.$$ But an analogous inequality for Stirling numbers of the first kind is missing, as remarked, for instance, in B.E. Sagan, Log-concave sequence of symmetric functions and analogs of the Jacobi Trudi determinants. Trans. Am. Math. Soc. 329 N°2 (1992) 795–811.

When $k=1$, since ${n\brack 1}= (n-1)!$, we have ${n\brack 1}^2 \le {n+1\brack 1}{n-1\brack 1}$, for $n \ge 2$.

Then, from numerical experimentation with larger $k$, it seems that we have log-convexity along the columns, that is $$ {n\brack k}^2 \le {n+1\brack k}{n-1\brack k},$$ provided that $k\ge 2$ and $n \ge \lfloor({\text e}-1)k\rfloor$, with $ {\text e}=2.71826 \cdots$. If true, this bound for $n$ would be sharp; indeed, there are $k$ for which the log-convexity inequality fails with $n=\lfloor({\text e}-1)k\rfloor-1$.

I am looking for a reference where this is established, or at least conjectured. If a proof (or disproof) is short enough to fit in an answer, I would welcome it as well.

Title: Intuitionistic interpretation of the Axiom of Infinity in ZF set theory
Body:
I'm self-studying ZF set theory and I've worked myself up to the set theoretic formalization of natural numbers. It seems like the standard approach to giving the natural numbers is to introduce the notion of inductive sets, and then introduce the Axiom of Infinity, that merely states that "there exists an inductive set", and then let the natural number be the least inductive set.

From an intuitionistic perspective, where existence claims that "such and such kind of object exists" is proven by providing a concrete object and proving that it is "such and such kind," it seems like the Axiom of Infinity cannot be accepted outright.

I don't mind the classical construction of the natural numbers, but it seems a bit of a round about construction to me. Why not merely have an axiom state that there exists a set N which includes 0 and s(n) if it includes n, and no other elements?

Is there a limitation in classical ZF that prevents us from saying "and no other elements" without doing the trick of regarding the intersection of all sets such that the elements of interest are included? (I.e. the way you usually state that the natural numbers is the smallest inductive set)

Title: Hundreds digit parity of prime squares and Chebyshev bias (Ilyosbek Hakimov's Conjecture)
Body:
Context and Motivation

I am investigating the distribution of prime numbers $p > 5$ partitioned into two sets modulo $20$:

  • Set A: $p \equiv 1, 3, 7, 9 \pmod{20}$
  • Set B: $p \equiv 11, 13, 17, 19 \pmod{20}$

By Dirichlet's theorem on arithmetic progressions, the primes are equally distributed asymptotically, implying: $$\lim_{N \to \infty} \frac{A(N)}{B(N)} = 1$$

However, numerical simulations up to $N = 1,000,000$ reveal a persistent bias where $A(N) < B(N)$ for most $N$.

My Work and Progress So Far

  1. Analytical Connection: This phenomenon appears to be a combined form of Chebyshev's Bias (or the prime number race). The residue classes in Set A and Set B correspond to quadratic non-residues / residues affecting the explicit formula for prime counting functions.
  2. Explicit Formula Approach: Using the logarithmic density and the Rubinstein–Sarnak framework, the distribution of $A(N) - B(N)$ depends on the zeroes of the Dirichlet $L$-functions $L(s, \chi)$ modulo 20.
  3. Simulation Details: I have implemented a verification script in Java to compute counts $A(N)$ and $B(N)$ up to $N = 10^6$, confirming that sign changes of $A(N) - B(N)$ are extremely rare in this range.

My Specific Questions

  1. Is there existing literature explicitly evaluating the logarithmic density $\delta(A < B)$ for this specific grouping modulo 20?
  2. How do non-trivial zeroes of $L(s, \chi)$ for characters mod 20 quantify the threshold for the first sign change of $A(N) - B(N)$ under the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) and Grand Simplicity Hypothesis (GSH)?

Title: Does there exist a pair of distinct triangles with equal area in the point sequence $P_n=(n,a^n)$ for $a=3$?
Body:
Let $a>0$, $a\neq 1$, and define the point sequence $$ P_n=(n,a^n),\qquad n\in\mathbb{Z}. $$ For $i<j<k$, the area of triangle $P_iP_jP_k$ is $$ S(i,j,k)=\frac{a^i}{2}\left|(j-i)(a^{k-i}-1)-(k-i)(a^{j-i}-1)\right|. $$

Case $a=2$. there is an explicit identity: $$ S(n,n+1,n+3)=S(n+2,n+3,n+4)=2^{n+1} $$ for every $n\in\mathbb{Z}$. Hence there are infinitely many pairs of distinct triangles with equal area.

However, when I searched for equal-area triangles in the case $a=3$, I found none. Can one prove that no two triangles have equal area for $a=3$, or find a counterexample?

More generally, for larger $a$, is there a general conclusion?

Incidentally, this problem is an extension of the slope problem. If no two triangles have equal area, then parallel chords cannot exist.

Title: The pro-$p$ completion of subgroups of principal congruence subgroups in $SL_n(\mathbb Z)$ for $n \ge 3$

Let $n \geq 3$. Let $\Gamma(m) = \{ A \in SL_n(\mathbb Z) : A \equiv I \mod m \}$ and let $H \leq \Gamma(p^k)$ for some $k \in \mathbb N$. Is the pro-$p$ completion of $H$ given by $\varprojlim_{n \to \infty} H / (H \cap \Gamma(p^n) )$?

Let $K \leq H$ be a subgroup of $H$ with $[H : K] = p^T$. It suffices to show that for some large $N$, $H \cap \Gamma(p^N) \leq K$. For this, it is enough to show that every $x \in H \cap \Gamma(p^N)$ is given by $g^{p^T}$ for some $g \in H$, then automatically $x \in K$.

Now I suppose if the map $g \to g^{p^T}$ from $H \cap \Gamma(p^{N-T})$ to $ H \cap \Gamma(p^N)$ was surjective, we'd be done. But, I don't see any reason why this would hold. We are not in a nice setting where $x \to x^p$ is an isomorphism between $\Gamma(p^N) \to \Gamma(p^{N+1})$; and even if this was the case, I don't see why $x^{p^T}$ would fall inside $H$.

If the answer to my question is no, are there any counterexamples?

Title: Is every accessible and coaccessible category necessarily essentially small?
Body:
It is well-known that a category that is locally presentable and locally copresentable is essentially small (and hence, thin). See Adamek-Rosicky, Thm. 1.64. Here, locally coporesentable means that the dual category is locally presentable.

I wonder if this is also true for the notion of accessiblity, i.e. when we drop colimits. Is every category that is accessible and coaccessible necessarily essentially small? Here, coaccessible means that the dual category is accessible.

CatDat currently has 118 categories, of which 42 are accessible and coaccessible (Search), but all of them are essentially small (Refined search). This motivates my question.

Such a result would be very helpful to disprove coaccessibility for various categories. If the result is not true, I would like to know counterexamples.

Title: Prove or disprove $\displaystyle\sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_n=1}^4\min\{x_{i_1}\cdots x_{i_n},y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_n}\}\ge(2+z)^{-n}$
Body:
Let $n\ge2$ be an integer, with $z\in(0,1)$ satisfying $\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk z^{\max(k,n-k)}=1$. Suppose $0\le x_i,y_i\le1/(2+z)$ for $i\in\{1,2,3,4\}$ and $\sum_{i=1}^4x_i=\sum_{i=1}^4y_i=1$.

My conjecture is that $$ \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_n=1}^4 \min\{x_{i_1}\cdots x_{i_n},y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_n}\} \ge\frac1{(2+z)^n}. $$ Equality holds at $(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)=(1,z,1,0)/(2+z)$ and $(y_1,y_2,y_3,y_4)=(0,1,z,1)/(2+z)$, where the sum equals $(2+z)^{-n}\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk z^{\max(k,n-k)}=(2+z)^{-n}$. Can the inequality be proved and all equality cases determined?

Attempt. From $\min\{x_i,y_i\}=x_i+y_i-\max\{x_i,y_i\}$, we obtain $\sum_{i=1}^4\min\{x_i,y_i\}\ge2-4/(2+z)=2z/(2+z)$. Therefore, $$ \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_n=1}^4 \min\{x_{i_1}\cdots x_{i_n},y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_n}\} \ge \left(\sum_{i=1}^4\min\{x_i,y_i\}\right)^n \ge \left(\frac{2z}{2+z}\right)^n. $$ However, $z<1/2$, and hence $(2z/(2+z))^n<(2+z)^{-n}$. For $n=2$, we have $z=(\sqrt3-1)/2$, and the inequality to prove is $\sum_{i,j=1}^4\min\{x_ix_j,y_iy_j\}\ge(1-1/\sqrt3)^2$.

Title: A cofinite-tail representation of negative numbers
Body:

One can define addition, subtraction etc. using recursion and the algebraic properties of integers would be the same. I am aware of closely related works in literature, but I did not find the same cofinite-tail representation.

Therefore, my question is:

$$ C_{x_0}^1=\cup_{\varepsilon>0}\{\psi\in C^1(I_{\varepsilon},V) : \psi(0)=x_0\},\quad I_{\varepsilon}=(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon) $$

For $\psi\in C_{x_0}^1$ and $f\in\mathcal{A}_1(V)$ we consider $g=f\circ\psi$. Then $g\in C^1(I_{\varepsilon},\mathbb{R})$ et we put $A_{x_0}(\psi,f)=\frac{dg}{dt}(0)$. We see that $A_{x_0}(\psi,\cdot)$ is linear and so we define the map $\tau_{x_0} : C_{x_0}^1\to(\mathcal{A}_1(V))^*$ defined by $\langle f,\tau_{x_0}(\psi)\rangle=A_{x_0}(\psi,f)$.

Hence, we define the tangent space at $V$ in $x_0$ to be the image of the map $\tau_{x_0}$. (For such definition we need to ensure that $\mathcal{A}_1(V)$ is not empty but it is not a problem for finite dimensional manifolds)

I first thought that the interest of this definition, instead of using the classical construction with tangent curves is that we do not refer to local charts. However, when we look at $A_{x_0}(\psi,f)$ we need to use local charts to have an expression of this, of course it does not depend on the local charts but anyway that takes away some of the interest in this definition for me since the classical construction by tangent curves does not depend on the local charts.

Title: Expressing a modified $\operatorname{dn}$-series in terms of elliptic integrals
Body:
For $h > 0$, let $g(t) = \cosh t \ln(2\cosh t) - t \sinh t$, and consider the sums $S_0(h) = \sum_{j \in \mathbb{Z}} g(jh)$ and $S_{1/2}(h) = \sum_{j \in \mathbb{Z}} g((j + 1/2)h)$. Can these sums be expressed in terms of Jacobi theta functions or elliptic integrals? I am particularly interested in $h = \ln 4$.

Since $g''(t) = g(t) - \operatorname{sech} t$, we obtain $$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(t) e^{-i\xi t} \, dt = \frac{\pi}{(1+\xi^2)\cosh(\pi\xi/2)}. $$ For $\varepsilon \in \{0, 1/2\}$, Poisson summation leads to $$ S_{\varepsilon}(h) = \frac{\pi}{h} \left[ 1 + 2 \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} \frac{\cos(2\pi m \varepsilon)}{\left(1 + \left(\frac{2\pi m}{h}\right)^2\right) \cosh\left(\frac{\pi^2 m}{h}\right)} \right]. \tag{1}\label{1} $$ Without the factor $1 + \left(\frac{2\pi m}{h}\right)^2$ in the denominator, the series is the Fourier series of the Jacobi function dn ($\operatorname{dn}$). More precisely, if $K = K(k)$, $K' = K\left(\sqrt{1-k^2}\right)$, and $K'/K = \pi/h$, then $$ \sum_{j \in \mathbb{Z}} \operatorname{sech}(jh + t) = \frac{2K}{h} \operatorname{dn}\left(\frac{2Kt}{h}, k\right). $$ Is there a corresponding expression for \eqref{1} that accounts for this factor $1 + \left(\frac{2\pi m}{h}\right)^2$?

Title: A polynomial lower bound for $-x\ln x-y\ln y-z\ln z$

Attempt. For $z=0$, we have $$ \mathrm{LHS}-\mathrm{RHS} =\sum_{k=3}^{\infty} \frac{(2x-1)^4-(2x-1)^{2k}}{2k(2k-1)} \ge0, $$ since $|2x-1|\le1$.

Title: Is a foliation induced by closed non-singular 1-form taut?
Body:
Let $M$ be an oriented compact 3-manifold with boundary and let $p:M\to{S}^{1}$ be a fibration. Let $\alpha$ be ${p}^{\ast}(\frac{1}{2\pi}d\theta)$ and clearly $\alpha$ is closed and non-singular. Now given a basis ${e}_{1},\dots,{e}_{k}$ of ${H}^{1}(M;\mathbb{R})$ and sufficiently small coefficients ${\delta}_{1},\dots,{\delta}_{k}$, we define $\alpha'=\alpha+\sum{\delta}_{i}{\alpha}_{i}$. This induces a codimension-one foliation $T\mathcal{F}=\ker(\alpha')$.

Question. Is this foliation a taut foliation?

Sketch of My Attempt. My idea is to reduce the problem to closed manifolds and there are powerful criterions such as the Rummler-Sullivan criterion. We want to work on the double $DM$. Define $\widehat{\alpha}={\widehat{p}}^{\ast}(\frac{1}{2\pi}d\theta)$ and $\widehat{\alpha}$ is closed and non-singular. By Mayer-Vietoris, we may extend $({e}_{i},{e}_{i})$ to ${\widehat{e}}_{i}\in{H}^{1}(DM;\mathbb{R})$. By de Rham theorem, there exist ${\eta}_{i}$ representing ${\widehat{e}}_{i}$. Let $r:DM\to DM$ be the diffeomorphism interchanging the two copies. Define ${\widehat{a}}_{i}=({\eta}_{i}+{r}^{\ast}{\eta}_{i})/2$, so ${\widehat{\alpha}}_{i}$ is closed and ${\widehat{\alpha}}_{i}{|}_{M}={\alpha}_{i}$. Finally, define ${\widehat{\alpha}}_{\delta}=\widehat{\alpha}+\sum{\delta}_{i}{\widehat{\alpha}}_{i}$. Similarly, it is closed and non-singular. It suffices to work on the foliation induced by ${\widehat{\alpha}}_{\delta}$. If it is taut, then $T\mathcal{F}$ is taut.

Now the Question reduces to: Is the foliation taut if the manifold has empty boundary?

Title: Difficult real world integration problem in thermodynamics
Body:

However, deriving Gibbs' free energy is proving to be a much more difficult integration problem and the only solutions that Wolfram is able to find use hypergeometric series but are valid only if the power law has a rational exponent. Precisely I am dealing with the following integral

$$G^R = \int_0^{x<1/a}\left(\frac{ab}{1-(1-ax)^b} - \frac{1}{x} \right)dx$$

where

  • $a$ is a real parameter greater than $1$ (more typically, they can be in the 3-5 range).
  • $b\in [0.2 , 0.3]$ he values for parameter b should include any real value between 0.2 and 0.3.

The integrand has definite values at both limits of integration so I know a real solution exists.

I have been able to generate solutions only with $b = 0.2$ ($1/5$) and $b = 0.25$ ($1/4$) using the Wolfram Alpha online integral calculator: nevertheless I am in need of a general solution for all real values of $b$ in $[0.2, 0.3]$ and $a > 1$.

Final notes

  • The limits of integration start at $x=0$.
  • The resulting Gibbs free energy equation should be a function of $x$ such that $x$ is no larger than $1/a$.

Thank you in advance for any new insight you can shed on this problem.

Title: Kruskal-Katona type result for sequence of maximal faces?
Body:

Now, similarly define the $f^{+}$-vector of a simplicial complex $\Delta$ for the number of maximal faces of each dimension/size, i.e. $$f^+_k = \#\{\sigma\in\Delta\,:\,|\sigma|=k\text{ and }\sigma\text{ is maximal}\}$$

Is there a similar characterizations of which $f^+$ vectors come from a simplicial complex? More precisely, I have two questions:

  • Given an integer $n$ and a vector $\mathbf{a}=(a_1,a_2,...)$, when does it exist a simplicial complex $\Delta$ on $n$ vertices with $f^+$-vector equal to $\mathbf{a}$ ?
  • Given an integer $n$ and two vectors $\mathbf{a}=(a_1,a_2,...)$ and $\mathbf{f}=(1, f_0, f_1,f_2,...)$, when does it exist a simplicial complex $\Delta$ on $n$ vertices with $f^+$-vector equal to $\mathbf{a}$ and $f$-vector equal to $\mathbf{f}$ ?

I'm expecting there to be some conditions akin to the one from Kruskal-Katona, but I can't find anything in the literature.

Title: Do three parallel chords exist in the point sequence $P_n=(n,a^n)$？
Body:
Let $a>0$, $a\neq 1$, and define the point sequence $$ P_n=(n,a^n),\qquad n\in\mathbb{Z} $$ A chord is a line segment joining two points $P_i$ and $P_j$ with $i<j$. Its slope is $$ k_{ij}=\frac{a^j-a^i}{j-i}. $$

For example, when $a=\sqrt{2}-1$, $$ k_{n,n+4}=k_{n+1,n+2} $$

In the example, parallel chords occur in pairs: each slope value is attained by exactly two distinct chords.

Does there exist an irrational $a>0$, $a\neq 1$, for which there are three distinct chords with the same slope?

In Rational cases, it is shown that no two distinct chords are parallel.

Title: Let ${\cal N}(m^n)$ denote the number of digits in $m^n$, if $m,n \in \mathbb N$, then proving ${\cal N}(2^n)+{\cal N}(5^n)={\cal N}(10^n)$
Body:
The question was to find the maximum natural number $n$ such that $${\cal N}(2^n)+{\cal N}(5^n)={\cal N}(10^n),\tag{$*$}$$ where ${\cal N}(m^n)$ denotes the number of digits in $m^n$, if $m,n \in \mathbb N$.

Noting the ${\cal N}(x)=1+[\log_{10} x]$, where $[.]$ denotes GIF (floor function) e.g., $[3.4]=3$. Then $(*)$ becomes $$2+[n\log_{10} 2]+[n\log_{10} 5]=1+n.$$ If $\log_{10}2=x$, then we get $$[nx]+[n-nx]=n-1 \implies n+[nx]+[-nx]=n-1.$$ If $z$ is non-integral, we have $[z]+[-z]=-1$, then eventually $(*)$ turns out to be an identity for all natural numbers $n$.

The question is: What could be other proofs of $(*)$, what could be other interesting generalizations of $(*)$?

Title: Numbers that are products of consecutive integers
Body:
I've been trying to find patterns in the frequency of numbers that are the product of at least two consecutive integers greater than 1, i.e. can be expressed as $_bP_a$ for $a,b\in\mathbb{N}$ and $1<a<b-1$.

For every $b$, there are $b-2$ possible values of $a$, which gives a crude estimate of $\sum_{n=3}^b n(n-2)=\frac13b^3-\frac12b^2-\frac56b+1$ such numbers that are less than $b!$.

However, this estimate has two sources of error. First, it doesn't count numbers such as $b(b+1)$, where the greatest in the sequence of factors is greater than $b$ but where the product itself is less than $b!$. The second source of error is that it will count numbers that can be written as the product of consecutive ingeters in multiple ways, for example $120=2\cdot3\cdot4\cdot5=4\cdot5\cdot6$.

The most common way for double counting to occur is in numbers of the form $_bP_a$ where $b=_{a-1}P_c$ for some $c$. The ways this can occur for any given $b$ is $\sum_{n=1}^{b-5}n=\frac12b^2-\frac92b+10$. Including this in our estimate gives $\frac13b^3+\frac{11}3b-9$ numbers less than $b!$ that can be written as the product of consecutive integers. Of course, this has overcorrected by removing instances that can be written in three different ways, if any exist.

I have a few related questions:

  1. Can triple counting, quadruple counting, etc., occur? If so, how can I adjust the estimate to account for this overcounting?

  2. Are there ways for double counting to occur other than what I found?

  3. How can I adjust my estimate to account for my first source of error?

Title: When does agreement of continuous functions on a set imply agreement on its closure? is Hausdorffness of the target space necessary?
Body:
Let $X,Y$ be topological spaces and let $f,g:X\to Y$ be two continuous functions. If $Y$ is Hausdorff It is not so hard to prove that; for every $A\subseteq X$ we have that $f\equiv g$ on $A$ implies $f\equiv g$ on $\bar{A}$.

To do so denote $\Lambda = \left\{ x\in X : f(x)=g(x) \right\}$. $f,g$ are two continuous function hence $F:X\to Y\times Y$ defined by $$F(x) = \left(f(x),g(x) \right)$$ is continuous. By the assumption $Y$ is Hausdorff, equivalently the diagonal $\Delta = \left\{ (y,y) : y\in Y \right\} \subseteq Y\times Y$ is closed in the product space. Notice that $\Lambda = F^{-1}\left(\Delta \right)$ hence by the continuity of $F$ it follows that $\Lambda \subseteq X$ is closed. Therefore, for every $A\subseteq X$ by the minimality of the closure we can deduce that $A\subseteq \Lambda \Longrightarrow \bar{A} \subseteq \Lambda$. $\blacksquare$

I have been trying generalize this result by relaxing the Hausdorffness assumption on $Y$. However, I haven't been able to either prove or come up with a counter example.

My question is, can the Hausdorffness assumption on $Y$ be relaxed? (please provide a proof/counter-example in either case).

A similar question has been asked here, however the linked question (as well as the answer) only discusses the case $Y$ is Hausdorff, which I already know. Thank you!

Title: Subbundles and quotients of non-split extensions of vector bundles
Body:
Let $X$ be a smooth complex projective surface, let $K$ and $Q$ be vector bundles over $X$.

Suppose that there exists a non-split extension $E$ of $Q$ via $K$, i.e. the following short sequence $$ 0\to K\to E\to Q\to0 $$ is exact.

Assume that $X$ is irreducible, let $\eta$ be its generic point. It is easy to prove that the generic fibre $E(\eta)$ is the direct sum of $K(\eta)$ and $Q(\eta)$, the generic fibres of $K$ and $Q$, respectively.

By [2, Proposition 1], there exists a unique saturated, torsion-free, coherent subsheaf $F$ of $E$ such that $F(\eta)$ is equal to $Q(\eta)$. By [1, Proposition 1], $F$ is a reflexive sheaf hence it is locally free ([1, Corollary 1.4]).

Question. Is $F$ isomorphic to $Q$?

[1] R. C. Hartshorne - Stable reflexive sheaves, Math. Ann. 254 (1980) 121-176.

[2] S. G. Langton - Valuative criteria for families of vector bundles on algebraic varieties, Ann. of Math. 101 (1975) 88-110.

Title: Can $\frac{bc-de}{b-d}$ give an odd integer when $bc-de=b^3-d^3$?
Body:
The question is, can $\frac{bc-de}{b-d}$ give an odd integer when $bc-de=b^3-d^3$? I tried to prove that it can not, but is the proof correct? Othervise, what is wrong?

I wanted to prove that equality in $bc-de=b^3-d^3$ is not possible when $b,c,d,e$, are positive pairwise coprime integers, everyone>1. Factorizing of the right side of $bc-de=b^3-d^3$ gives $bc-de=(b-d)(b-d)^2-3bd$; $\frac{bc-de}{b-d}=(b-d)^2-3bd$. The right side always is odd, since $b$ and $d$ both are odd, or one of them is odd, the other is even. Both can not be even since they are coprimes.

Let the right side $=u$. Assume that $u$ is a positive odd integer, $u>1$. Then $\frac{bc-de}{b-d}=u$; $bc-de=u(b-d)$; $bc-de=bu-du$; $bc-bu=de-du$; $b(c-u)=d(e-u)$; Since $b$ and $d$ are coprimes, there is $b=e-u$ and $d=c-u$. Then $u=e-b$ and $u=c-d$. But since $b,c,d,e$ are positive pairwise coprime integers, only one of them can be even. Then either the right sides of both $u=e-b$ and $u=c-d$ are even, or one of the right sides is odd and one is even. Both cases make contradictions. The assumption that $u$ is an odd integer leads to a contradiction. Then the equation $bc-de=b^3-d^3$ has no integer solutions.

Title: Is the proof of $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1$ circular when developing calculus from first principles
Body:
I found the related question [Non-Circular Proof of $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1$], but I think my question is slightly different.

I'm not just looking for a proof that avoids derivatives. I'm trying to understand the foundational order of the definitions and theorems involved.

The usual geometric argument is

$$ \sin x < x < \tan x $$

for $0<x<\pi/2$, which gives

$$ \cos x < \frac{\sin x}{x}<1 $$

and hence

$$ \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1. $$

But I'm wondering what has to be established before this argument is actually rigorous.

In particular:

What is the rigorous definition of $\sin x$ when $x$ is an arbitrary real number? How do we rigorously define the radian measure $x$ without already using analytic properties of the trigonometric functions? When we say that an arc subtending an angle $x$ on the unit circle has length $x$, what theorem establishes this? If we define $\sin$ using an integral (or define $\arcsin$ using an integral and then take its inverse), that avoids circularity only by choosing a particular analytic definition. What is the minimal set of assumptions needed for that construction? Is there a standard foundational development of the real numbers, arc length, trigonometric functions, limits, and integration in which

$$ \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1 $$

is proved before the derivative formulas for $\sin$ and $\cos$, with no circular reasoning?

I'm especially interested in the distinction between:

avoiding circularity in a particular proof, and establishing that the definitions and preceding results themselves do not depend, directly or indirectly, on $\lim_{x\to0}\sin x/x=1$.

The latter is what I'm really trying to understand.

Title: A sharp refinement of a fractional-power inequality
Body:
For $1<r\le5$ and $0<t<1$, let $\mathbf x=(x_1,\ldots,x_4)$ and $\mathbf y=(y_1,\ldots,y_4)$ satisfy $0\le x_1\le\cdots\le x_4\le r$, $0\le y_1\le\cdots\le y_4\le r$, and $\sum_{i=1}^4x_i=\sum_{i=1}^4y_i=2r+1$. With $\mathbf v=(v_1,\ldots,v_4)=(0,1,r,r)$, does $$ \sum_{i=1}^4x_i^t y_{5-i}^{1-t} \ge r^t+r^{1-t} + \frac{r+1-r^t-r^{1-t}}{(r-1)^2} \sum_{i=1}^4\left[(x_i-v_i)^2+(y_i-v_i)^2\right] $$ hold for all such $\mathbf x,\mathbf y$?

For $t=1/2$, the proposed inequality simplifies to $$ \sum_{i=1}^4\sqrt{x_i y_{5-i}} \ge 2\sqrt r+ \frac{1}{(1+\sqrt r)^2} \sum_{i=1}^4\left[(x_i-v_i)^2+(y_i-v_i)^2\right]. $$ At $\mathbf x=\mathbf y=(0,(r+1)/2,(r+1)/2,r)$, we have $\sum_{i=1}^4x_i^t y_{5-i}^{1-t}=r+1$ and $\sum_{i=1}^4[(x_i-v_i)^2+(y_i-v_i)^2]=(r-1)^2$.

Title: An inequality for ${}_2F_1$ involving $\operatorname{erfc}$
Body:
This question arose from my earlier question, where the optimal coefficient is $C(x)=x(1+x)(1+4x+x^2)/(1-x)^5$. Since $C(x)\to\infty$ as $x\uparrow1$, I am looking for a bound that remains finite there.

For an integer $n\ge1$ and $t>0$, does $$ \begin{aligned} 0\le{}& {}_2F_1(1,-n;n+1;-e^{-t}) -\frac1{1-e^{-t}}+\frac1t\\ &-\frac{\sqrt{\pi n}}2 e^{nt^2/4}\operatorname{erfc}\left(\frac{\sqrt n\,t}{2}\right) \le \frac{1-\sqrt\pi/2}{\sqrt n} \end{aligned} $$ hold?

My attempt starts from $$ {}_2F_1(1,-n;n+1;-e^{-t}) = \sum_{j=0}^n \frac{\binom{2n}{n+j}}{\binom{2n}{n}}e^{-jt}. $$ The approximation $\binom{2n}{n+j}/\binom{2n}{n}\approx e^{-j^2/n}$ suggests using $$ \begin{aligned} \int_0^\infty e^{-u^2/n-tu}\,du &=\frac{\sqrt{\pi n}}2 e^{nt^2/4}\operatorname{erfc}\left(\frac{\sqrt n\,t}{2}\right),\\ \sum_{j=0}^{\infty}e^{-jt}-\int_0^\infty e^{-tu}\,du &=\frac1{1-e^{-t}}-\frac1t. \end{aligned} $$ The proposed constant $1-\sqrt\pi/2$ comes from $n=1$ and $t\downarrow0$.

Title: Is this degree weight lower bound for parity of conjunctions known?
Body:
Let $u,k\ge 1$ be integers, and split $uk$ Boolean variables into $k$ blocks of size $u$. Define $$ f(x)=\prod_{\ell=1}^{k}\left(1-2\prod_{j=1}^{u}x_{\ell,j}\right). $$

Suppose $$ P(x)=\sum_C a_C C(x), $$ where each $C$ is a conjunction of at most $D$ distinct literals, possibly including negated literals, and the coefficients are real. Assume $f(x)P(x)\ge 1$ for every Boolean input. Write $L=\sum_C |a_C|$.

I obtain $$ L\ge \left(\frac{2uk}{D}\right)^k \qquad (1\le D\le uk). $$

Here is the argument. Independently in each block, choose the all-one vector with probability $1/2$; otherwise choose a uniformly random vector with exactly one zero.

For a conjunction using $s_\ell$ variables in block $\ell$, its correlation with that block's signed AND has magnitude at most $s_\ell/(2u)$:

  • With only positive literals, the correlation is $-s_\ell/(2u)$.
  • With exactly one negative literal, it is $1/(2u)$.
  • With two or more negative literals, it is zero.
  • An unqueried block also has zero correlation.

Contradictory conjunctions are identically zero and can be discarded.

Independence and AM–GM therefore give $$ \left|\mathbb{E}[fC]\right| \le \prod_{\ell=1}^{k}\frac{s_\ell}{2u} \le \left(\frac{D}{2uk}\right)^k. $$

Consequently, $$ 1\le \mathbb{E}[fP] \le L\left(\frac{D}{2uk}\right)^k, $$ which proves the claimed bound.

Is this argument valid, including for conjunctions containing negated literals? Is there a reference for this bound or a stronger known version?

I am asking about this specific representation bound, not claiming a general circuit lower bound or a P versus NP result.

Title: Construction of interpolation space: some intuition?
Body: When studying interpolation of normed vector spaces, one defines the family of norms over $X_0 + X_1$: $K(x,t) := \inf \{\Vert x_0 \Vert_{X_0} + t \Vert x_1 \Vert_{X_1} \ | \ x = x_0 + x_1 \}$ which basically weights how much we value the second norm. Then one observes some nice properties of this family: as a function of $t$, $K(x,t)$ is increasing, concave and $t^{-1}K(x,t) = K(x,t^{-1})$. Concavity here implies that taking any convex combination of the two starting norms always sits below $K(x,t)$, which I suppose is a nice fact that tells you you don't need to bother with choosing a convex combination of the starting norms as a norm on $X_0 + X_1$, as $K(x,t)$ already sits above all those. The scaling property is more obscure to me, so if there is some nice way to see why it matters I'd love to hear it. Going forward, one now considers, for fixed $\sigma \in (0,1)$ and fixed $x \in X_0 + X_1$, the function $\psi(t) := \frac{K(x,t)}{t^{\sigma}} = K(x,\frac{1}{t^{\sigma}})$. Then we define $$\Vert x \Vert_{\sigma, q}^q := \int_0^{+\infty} (K(x,t))^q \, \frac{dt}{t^{1+\sigma q}} = \Vert \psi \Vert_{L^q((0, +\infty); \frac{dt}{t})}^q.$$ Here I'm lost to say the least. What does this norm do? What is it "weighting"? Expecially, why are we integrating $\psi$ in $\frac{dt}{t}$?

Title: Can the Hadamard-cube identities force the nonexistence of a fourth MUB in $\mathbb{C}^6$?
Body:
Note: Users attempting to answer this question please once go through the paper linked here: Triplets of mutually unbiased bases - Máté Matolcsi, Ákos K. Matszangosz, Dániel Varga and Mihály Weiner

Let $X_1,X_2,X_3$ be three mutually unbiased orthonormal bases of $\mathbb C^6$.

Definitions $$ H_1=\sqrt{6}\,X_1^*X_2\qquad\\ H_2=\sqrt{6}\,X_2^*X_3\qquad\\ H_3=\sqrt{6}\,X_3^*X_1\qquad $$ Thus each $H_j$ is a $6\times6$ complex Hadamard matrix.

For a complex Hadamard matrix $H$ with columns $h_1,\ldots,h_6$, and $ \gamma=(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_6)\in\mathbb Z^6, $ let me define $$ g_H(\gamma) = \sum_{k=1}^6 \prod_{r=1}^6(H_{rk})^{\gamma_r}, $$ $$ G_H(\gamma)=|g_H(\gamma)|^2, $$ $$ \widetilde G_H(\gamma) = \sum_{\pi\in S_6}G_H(\pi(\gamma)). $$

Consider these further definitions of $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$: $$ \gamma_1=(1,1,1,-1,-1,-1) \qquad \gamma_2=(3,3,3,-3,-3,-3)\qquad $$

The paper which I linked at the top conjectures that every MUB-triplet in $\mathbb C^6$ satisfies $$ \begin{aligned} &\widetilde G_{H_1}(\gamma_1) +\widetilde G_{H_2}(\gamma_1) +\widetilde G_{H_3}(\gamma_1)\\ &\quad+ \widetilde G_{H_1}(\gamma_2) \widetilde G_{H_1^*}(\gamma_2) + \widetilde G_{H_2}(\gamma_2) \widetilde G_{H_2^*}(\gamma_2) + \widetilde G_{H_3}(\gamma_2) \widetilde G_{H_3^*}(\gamma_2) =0. \end{aligned} $$

Question: Can this identity be proved directly from the orthogonality and mutual-unbiasedness relations defining $X_1,X_2,X_3$?

Can it be derived algebraically from the defining identities of the associated Hadamard cube, perhaps by using polynomial identities or Gröbner-basis techniques?

Title: The "Immersion lemma" in Freedman & Quinn

This immersion lemma is that a map of a disk (or R $\times$ I) that extends to a framed immersion on the boundary, can be homotoped rel boundary to a map which extends to a framed immersion, which near the boundary differs from the original map by rotations or signs. The second part is that if a surface is the union of two open sets, and the restriction of the immersion to the opens sets extend to framed immersions agreeing on the intersection, then the immersion can be isotoped to a map which extends to a framed immersion of the whole surface.

They say that the lemma is a simple case of transversality, and that it is proved in many textbooks. Is there a specific reference for a book which proves this lemma completely?

Title: How to find $\int_0^1 \left(\frac{\sinh^{-1} x}{x}\right)^n \, dx$?

Title: Well-foundedness and using it, is it true that Well Ordering Principle always implies Induction?
Body:
This Springer link gives, at page $34$, five Peano axioms :

Let $N$ be a set, $S$ a function $S: N\rightarrow N$ and $0$ an object, the five axioms are:

  1. $0 \in N$
  2. If $n\in N$, then $S(n) \in N$
  3. No element of $N$ has $0$ as a sucessor
  4. If $S(n)=S(m)$, then $n=m$
  5. If $S\subseteq N$ such that $0\in S$ and $\forall m\in S$, we have $S(m) \in S$, then $S=N$

The paper also gives an additional axiom:

5'. Every non-empty subset of $N$ has a least element.

Questions: what is the underlying partial order in the above axioms? Is it $m \leq n \iff \exists k\geq 1, n=S^k (m)$ or $n=m$ ? What is the link with Well-Foundedness (the absence of infinite and strictly decreasing sequence in the partial order)?

Also, the Jean Gallier's notes from University of Penn. say that Well-Foundedness implies (5).

I've proved that Well-Foundedness is equivalent to "every non-empty subset of the poset has a minimal element". So we can draw the conclusion that (5') implies Well-Foundedness.

So (5') always implies (5)?

But the paper says:

In the axiomatic system consisting of axioms (1)–(4) together with axiom (5'), induction (5) can’t be a theorem, since there is a model Ord in which all these five axioms are satisfied, but induction (5) is not true.

Title: How does the topology of Tangora's connected space depend on the choice of partition $A,B,C$?
Body:
Tangora's connected space (see here) is the space $X=\mathbb R$ with the following topology.

Partition $\mathbb{R}$ into three dense sets $A, B, C$. The topology on $X$ is generated by the usual open intervals, the sets $A, B$, and sets of the form $\{c\}\cup ((x, y)\setminus C)$ with $c\in C$ and $x<c<y$.

It was described by Tangora in Solution 5242 of American Mathematical Monthly, to provide an example of a connected space that is the union of two closed totally disconnected subspaces. It is example #133 in Counterexamples in topology, also recorded in pi-base.

How does the topology of $X$ depend on the choice of $A, B, C$?
Determining all homeomorphism classes of such spaces is probably too a hard question to solve. (One observation: The set $C$ is closed and discrete. It is likely that choosing sets $C$ with different cardinalities would yield non-homeomorphic spaces.)

A simpler question:

If $A$ and $B$ are chosen to be countable, are all resulting spaces $X$ homeomorphic?

Title: Seeking an example of a proof "architecture" that leverages a bijection from $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}$ to generalize a result about two variables

  • First, a result (perhaps about a function) is demonstrated in two real variables.

  • Then, because there is a bijection from $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}$, the second input variable (real) can actually "represent" $n$ variables.

Title: Why is $\sum_{i=1}^{n} i$ associated with $O(n^2)$ if evaluating it takes $O(n)$ time?
Body:
I am trying to understand the distinction between the growth of a mathematical function and the time complexity of an algorithm. I was told in class the Time completizty is basically us estimated how long it takes to run an algorithim, along those lines.

Consider the sum

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n} i = 1+2+3+\cdots+n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}. $$

Its value grows quadratically with $n$, since

$$ \frac{n(n+1)}{2} = \frac{n^2+n}{2} = \Theta(n^2). $$

However, if I calculate the sum directly by adding each term, I only need $n$ additions:

sum = 0
for i = 1 to n:
    sum = sum + i

This appears to take $\Theta(n)$ time because the loop performs $n$ iterations. (Was told this in class)

Alternatively, using the closed-form expression

$ \frac{n(n+1)}{2}, $

it appears to take $\Theta(1)$ arithmetic operations, assuming that addition and multiplication each take constant time.

So what exactly does it mean to say that

$ \sum_{i=1}^{n} i $

is $O(n^2)$?

Is $O(n^2)$ referring only to the growth rate of the value of the function, rather than the time required to evaluate it?

Also, consider the following nested loop:

for i = 1 to n:
    for j = 1 to i:
        do_constant_work()

Its total amount of work is

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n} i = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} = \Theta(n^2). $$

Why does this summation represent $\Theta(n^2)$ time in the nested-loop example, while directly calculating the same summation appears to take only $\Theta(n)$ time?

I would especially like to understand the distinction between:

  1. the growth rate of a mathematical function;
  2. the number of terms in a summation;
  3. the time required to evaluate the summation;
  4. the time complexity of a nested loop.

Title: Tangora's space is connected
Body:
In issue 5242 of Mathematical American Monthly, it was asked if a union of two closed totally disconnected subspaces must be totally disconnected. The answer is no, and the issue presents three solutions. Tangora gave the following example:

Partition $\mathbb{R}$ into three dense sets $A, B, C$. Define the topology on $X = \mathbb{R}$ to be the one generated by open intervals, $A, B$, and sets of the form $\{c\}\cup ((x, y)\setminus C)$ with $c\in C$ and $x<c<y$. Then $X\setminus A, X\setminus B$ are closed and totally disconnected and $X = (X\setminus A)\cup (X\setminus B)$ is connected.

It's easy to see why $X\setminus A, X\setminus B$ are totally disconnected, this is proven in the same way as zero-dimensionality of $\mathbb{Q}$ or $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$. On the other hand, Tangora claims that connectedness of $X$ can be proven just like the usual connectedness of $\mathbb{R}$, by its least upper bound property, one just has to consider cases. Can someone give an explicit argument?

Title: Best known explicit lower bounds for prime gaps
Body:
X-Posted to SO

The classical construction showing that prime gaps can be unbounded is considering the numbers $n!+2,\cdots,n!+n$, this outputs $n-1$ consecutive composite numbers, and so, prime gaps can be arbitrarily large. Letting

$$G(x)=\max_{p_n\leq x} (p_{n}-p_{n-1})$$

this proof gives a lower bound of the type

$$G(x)\gtrsim\frac{\log x}{\log\log x}.$$

This bound has been improved many times, the best known one as I'm writing this post is

$$G(x)\gtrsim\frac{\log _2^2x\log_4 x}{\log_3 x}\log x$$

where $\log_tx$ denotes the $t$-th iterated logarithm. As far as I understand, this latter bound, and the couple best known before it, were probabilistic arguments, and therefore non-explicit. My question is what's the best known explicit lower bound? The first bound given above can be beaten by taking the numbers $n\#+2,\cdots,n\#+n$ where

$$n\#=\prod_{p\leq n}p$$

this giving a lower bound of

$$G(x)\gtrsim\log x$$

at this point one may wonder what exactly qualifies as "explicit", for definiteness say, that for every $n$ one can find a number $f(n)$ in polynomial time such that $f(n),f(n)+1,\cdots,f(n)+n-1$ are all composite. Thus, the two explicit bounds I gave above are indeed explicit.

As far as I understand Rankin's proof of

$$G(x)\gtrsim\frac{\log_2 x\log_4x}{\log_3^2x}\log x$$

is via a greedy algorithm, so it should also be explicit, though saying it for certain would require one to go through a complexity analysis of their algorithm. Is this where the story ends? Since Rankin's bound was beaten has there been any work on explicit lower bounds (like it has been the case for other hard to compute functions, such as Ramsey numbers)?

Title: Geometric conditions forcing a separable transitive Banach space to be Hilbertian
Body:
I am currently going through a research paper Transitivity of the Norm on Banach Spaces by Julio Becerra Guerrero and A. Rodríguez-Palacios given here, and where the following question is derived. It is not exactly present in the paper, but the framework is similar:

Let $X$ be an infinite-dimensional separable Banach space, and let $S_X$ denote its unit sphere.

Suppose that $X$ is transitive, meaning that for every $x,y\in S_X$, there exists a surjective linear isometry $$ T:X\to X $$ such that $ T(x)=y. $

It is known that every Hilbert space is transitive, while the converse in the separable infinite-dimensional case is the famous Banach--Mazur rotation problem.

A transitive separable Banach space is known to satisfy several strong geometric properties like separability together with transitivity implies smoothness of the norm.

The Question is:

Suppose $X$ is a separable transitive Banach space. Which additional geometric assumptions on $X$ are sufficient to force $X$ to be Hilbertian?

Let me frame the question better:

If $X$ is separable and transitive, and its unit ball has normal structure (or, alternatively, is dentable), does this already imply that $X$ is isometric to a Hilbert space?

If this is known, what is the sharpest theorem currently available, and where is the essential obstruction in attempting to remove the additional geometric hypothesis?

Can anyone help?

Title: Proving positivity the solution of a Predator-Prey model
Body:
Consider the following predator-prey system: $$ \begin{cases} \dfrac{dN}{dT} &= rN\left(1-\dfrac{N}{K(T)}\right) -aN^\alpha P -\dfrac{qEN}{mE+nN},\\ \dfrac{dP}{dT} &=-d_1P+aeN^\alpha P. \end{cases} $$ where all parameters are positive, $0<\alpha<1$, and $K(T)>0$.

Question. Suppose that $ N(0)>0$, and $P(0)>0$. I want to prove that $$ N(T)\geq0,\qquad P(T)>0 $$ for all $T\geq0$ for which the solution exists.
For the predator equation, $$ \frac{dP}{dT} = \left(-d_1+aeN^\alpha\right)P, $$ so $$ P(T) = P(0)\exp\left( \int_0^T[-d_1+aeN(s)^\alpha]\,ds \right). $$ Thus, provided the integral is finite on every finite interval of existence, $$ P(0)>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad P(T)>0. $$ The difficulty is the prey equation. For $N>0$, it can be written as $$ \frac{dN}{dT} = N\left[ r\left(1-\frac{N}{K(T)}\right) -aPN^{\alpha-1} -\frac{qE}{mE+nN} \right]. $$ If $0<\alpha<1$, then $$ N^{\alpha-1}\to\infty \qquad\text{as }N\to0^+. $$ Therefore, the usual integrating-factor argument for equations of the form $N'=g(T)N$ does not immediately work here.

Title: Possible formalisations of an Orwellian problem
Body:
I am a high-school math teacher. I am currently designing a mathematical-logic problem inspired by Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four. The Orwellian setting is only motivation; I am interested in the underlying formal system.

Suppose we have a collection of agents and a set of propositions currently required by an organisation. An agent commits thoughtcrime if they independently judge a proposition and reach a conclusion incompatible with what is currently required.

For every agent who commits thoughtcrime:

  • P1: They must come to accept whatever is currently required.
  • P2: They must then be able to replace an accepted proposition with an incompatible one when required.
  • P3: They may be removed only after P1 and P2 have been achieved.
  • P4: There must always remain enough agents to apply P1–P3 to every subsequent offender.

Assume also that a distinguished administrator can detect thoughtcrime, distinguish genuine judgment from pretence, and force agents through P1 and P2. I take these abilities as axioms.

My main questions are:

  1. What is the appropriate formal framework? Should this be modelled as a transition system, temporal/modal logic, belief revision, a fixed-point problem, or something else? What assumptions would need to be changed to make the system formally well-defined?

  2. Can the rules themselves lead to an infinite regress of agents? For example, if determining whether agent (a) has committed thoughtcrime requires another agent (b) to make an independent judgment, and determining whether (b) has committed thoughtcrime requires another agent (c), can this process continue indefinitely? If such a regress can occur, does it create a genuine logical obstruction?

Ultimately, I want to know whether P1–P4 can be simultaneously satisfied under an appropriate formalisation, and what mathematical framework is best suited to determining this.

Title: Do the Lusternik-Schnirelmann eigenvalues exhaust the spectrum of the $p$-Laplacian?
Body:
Let $\Omega\subset\Bbb R^d$ be bounded and open. let $\Delta_p u = \text{div}(|\nabla u|^{p-2}\nabla u)$, $1<p<\infty$. For the Dirichlet $p$-Laplacian,

$$-\Delta_p u = \lambda |u|^{p-2}u \quad \text{in } \Omega, \quad u = 0 \quad \text{on } \partial\Omega,$$ it is well known that one can construct using the using the Lusternik-Schnirelmann principle an increasing sequence of variational eigenvalues $$0 < \lambda_1(p) \le \lambda_2(p) \le \dots, \quad \lambda_k(p) \to \infty.$$ For $p = 2$, the spectral theorem implies that this sequence (counting multiplicities) exhausts the entire spectrum. That is $\sigma (-\Delta)= (\lambda_n)_n$.

Question: For $p \neq 2$, does the sequence $\{\lambda_k(p)\}_{k \ge 1}$ exhaust the entire spectrum of the $p$-Laplacian, or can there exist eigenvalues that are not captured by this variational sequence?

Title: Multivariable calculus on affine space
Body:
I am taking a multivariable calculus course at university. We have been told that in $f: \mathbb{R}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$, both $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\mathbb{R}^m$ are vector spaces.

I understand that we need some sort of structure to be able to operate with them, as otherwise they would be just n-tuples, but instead of vector spaces we could consider them affine spaces. In my opinion, it is more general than a vector space, and offers more opportunities. Does that work? Does it change anything?

Every operation (especially regarding differentiation) would be well described, and we could further distinguish between points and vectors, other than just n-tuples.

There was a very very similar question posted here almost 11 years ago, that sums up most of my doubts, but I don't quite understand the answers given. Why don't we consider $\mathbb{R}^3$ to be an affine space?

Thank you very much. If you know some material to build up on this, I will be thankful.

Edit 1: Doing some more research, reading the recommended related questions, I have seen that we could interpret a function as something that relates $p$ to $f(p)$, both being points (although they can be represented by vectors), but in order to do calculus, we need a tangent space associated to that point. Is this correct?

Edit 2: Reading the comments, and thinking a bit about it, it is perfectly possible to do vector calculus only on a vector space. As long as you have a norm, everything is defined to formally do calculus. The issue is that you may not be able to represent it on a plane, because, for that, the structure of an affine space is necessary. For example, you can calculate the gradient with only a vector space, but it cannot be represented unless it is affine because it needs a point of application.

Title: how to prove $p_0/p_1$ is conditional expectation of $dq/dp$
Body:
Consider the SDE

\begin{cases} dX_t^1=u(X_t^1,X_t^2)\,dt+dB_t,\\[2mm] dX_t^2=X_t^1\,dt,\\[2mm] (X_0^1,X_0^2)=x\in\mathbb{R}^2, \end{cases}

where $u:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ is bounded. Suppose that, under $\mathbb P$, the law of $X_t=(X_t^1,X_t^2)$ has density $p_1(t,x,z)$.

Define

$$ M_t=\exp\left(-\int_0^t u(X_s)\,dB_s-\frac12\int_0^t |u(X_s)|^2\,ds\right) $$

and define $\mathbb Q$ on $\mathcal F_t$ by $d\mathbb Q/d\mathbb P=M_t$. Since $u$ is bounded, Novikov's condition holds. Hence, by Girsanov's theorem,

$$ \overline B_t=B_t+\int_0^t u(X_s)\,ds $$

is a Brownian motion under $\mathbb Q$. Therefore, under $\mathbb Q$, the process satisfies $$dX_t^1=d\overline B_t$$ and $$dX_t^2=X_t^1,dt$$, so the law of $X_t$ has the Kolmogorov density $p_0(t,x,z)$.

my question is: How can I prove rigorously that $$ \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[M_t\mid X_t=z\right]=\frac{p_0(t,x,z)}{p_1(t,x,z)} $$ for $p_1(t,x,z),dz$-almost every $z$? In particular, how should the ratio be defined on the set where $p_1(t,x,z)=0$? I am not yet sure why $p_0(t,x,z)$ must also vanish almost everywhere on that set.

Title: What is the smallest multivariate polynomial $p$ so that $p[\mathbb Z\times\dots\times \mathbb Z] = \mathbb N$
Body:
We know by Lagrange's four-square theorem that every non-negative integer can be written as the sum of four square numbers. This means to say $$\{a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2: a, b, c, d\in\mathbb Z\} = \mathbb N.$$

This motivates my question: what is the smallest multivariate polynomial $p$ so that $p[\mathbb Z\times\dots\times \mathbb Z] = \mathbb N$? 'Small' in this context means 'with a small degree and a small number of variables'. The solution $p(x, y, z, w)\equiv x^2+y^2+z^2+w^2$ is actually quite small, only having degree two and four variables; but is it the smallest?

It is easy to see no polynomial of degree one and no polynomial of one variable can accomplish the task, so the smallest degree is definitely two.

Title: Computationally efficient algorithm for multivector inverses.
Body:
I am currently writing a code library for geometric algebra, just as a side project, as a way of better understanding both programming an geometric algebra. I now face the hurdle of finding the inverse of multivectors. Currently I am just working with multivectors with signature $(d,0)$. For $d\le5$, the paper https://doi.org/10.1016/j.amc.2017.05.027 provides some algorithms for this, however for $d>5$, everything I can find seems to point to converting multivectors to matrices and inverting those. However, it seems that the matrix representation of a multivector is $2^{d}\times2^{d}$. Given that matrix inversion is $M^{-1}\in\mathcal{O}\left(n^{\log_{2}(7)}\right)$, it directly implies that $v^{-1}\in\mathcal{O}\left(7^{n}\right)$, which is ludicrously slow for something as used as calculating inverses.

I am wondering if there is some other algorithm for finding multivector inverses that works better for computers, I find it hard to believe that $\mathcal{O}\left(7^{n}\right)$ is the best possible method. I know the aforementioned paper lists a few isomorphisms, however as far as I can tell they either relate clifford algebras different signatures, or relate clifford algebras to matrix algebras, neither of which seems to be particularly helpful for algorithms that computers can calculate sufficiently quickly.

Title: About $T_0$ space
Body:

  1. The topology of $X$ is finer than the cofinite topology on $X$.
  2. For every $x \in X$, $X \setminus \{x\}$ is open.
  3. Every finite subset of $X$ is closed.
  4. $X$ is Hausdorff.

Consider the Sierpiński space $X = \{a, b\}$ with topology $\mathcal{T} = \{\emptyset, \{a\}, \{a, b\}\}$.

Title: Laplace formula for the resolvent operator
Body:
I am currently investigating the properties of the resolvent operator $R(\lambda, A) = (\lambda I - A)^{-1}$. Specifically, I am focusing on the Laplace representation of the resolvent, which is expressed as:

$$R(\lambda, A) = \int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t} T(t) dt\, ,$$

where $T(t) = e^{At}$ is the heat flow of the generator $A$. I have a few interrelated questions regarding the domain of validity of this formula, its analytic continuation, and its concrete application.

  1. Is the Laplace formula for the resolvent strictly valid only within a specific region of the resolvent set $\rho(A)$? For instance, I think is valid in the half-plane $\text{Re}(\lambda) > \omega$ for a quasi-bounded exponential semigroup. The wikipedia page on the resolvent formalism states that instead of taking the positive real half-line, for a general complex number lambda we can take the half-line $\arg(\lambda) = - \arg(t)$, but then does the heat kernel has to be intended in its complex extension? What does this mean?

  2. Suppose the integral converges only in a proper subregion $\Omega \subset \rho(A)$. Given that the resolvent operator $\lambda \mapsto R(\lambda, A)$ is analytic on the entire set $\rho(A)$, is it standard practice to extend the formula obtained in $\Omega$ to the whole resolvent set via analytic continuation? Do we lose the integral representation of the resolvent outside of $\Omega$?

  3. Could you provide some guidance or references on how this approach applies to the Laplacian $A = -\Delta$? Specifically, how do the convergence region of the integral and its subsequent analytic continuation manifest when deriving the classical free resolvent kernel?

Any insights, rigorous justifications, or standard bibliographic references would be highly appreciated.

Thank you in advance for your time and help.

Title: Intersection of set-valued two functors
Body:
The original motivation behind this question comes from an exercise in Vakil's The Rising Sea (Ex. 2.2.G).

Suppose we are given a continuous map $\mu: Y\to X$. Show that “sections of $\mu$” form a sheaf. More precisely, to each open set $U$ of $X$, associate the set of continuous maps $s: U\to Y$ such that $\mu \circ s=\mathrm{id}_{U}$. Show that this forms a sheaf.

I noticed that I can see this functor succinctly as $\mathrm{Hom}_\mathsf{Top} (-,Y)\cap \mu_*^{-1}(\mathrm{id}_{(-)})$. The first functor should of course be clear. We define the second functor as follows. For each open set $U\subseteq X$ we take the set $$\mu_*^{-1}(\mathrm{id}_{U})=\{f\in \mathrm{Hom}_\mathsf{Top} (X,Y)\mid \mu\circ f|_U=\mathrm{id}_U \},$$ and for each inclusion $V\hookrightarrow U$ we consider the "restriction" $\mu_*^{-1}(\mathrm{id}_{U})\to \mu_*^{-1}(\mathrm{id}_{V})$ given by post-composition by said inclusion. This works because restricting the identity on $U$ to $V$ gives the identity on $V$, though I think we have to get a corestriction involved since the codomains do not really match....well.

  1. Aside from the fact that this is supposed to be a sheaf, why should I expect to be functorial? Namely, is the intersection of two set-valued functors also a functor?
  2. If yes, when are these functors representable?

Also, as an additional question, is the $\mu_*^{-1}(\mathrm{id}_{(-)})$ functor representable?

Title: Clique Size in the $(2:2)$ Maker-Breaker Game
Body:
Let $K_N$ be the complete graph on $N$ vertices. Consider the $(2:2)$ Maker--Breaker game on the edges of $K_N$: Maker and Breaker alternately claim two previously unclaimed edges, with Maker moving first. Maker wins if the graph formed by the claimed edges contains a clique $K_q$.

In the ordinary $(1:1)$ game, Beck proved that the largest clique Maker can force has order $$ (2-o(1))\log_2 N $$ In fact the conjectured second-order threshold is $ q=2\log_2 N-2\log_2\log_2 N+O(1). $

I am asking whether the same random-graph threshold persists when both players are given twice the bias.

Let me simplify it. In the $(2:2)$ Maker--Breaker clique game on $K_N$, is it true that $$ q=2\log_2 N-2\log_2\log_2 N+O(1) $$ is the threshold for the largest clique Maker can force? Or can Maker force a $K_q$ for $$ q=2\log_2 N-2\log_2\log_2 N+O(1), $$ while Breaker can prevent Maker from obtaining such a clique (with the appropriate interpretation of the $O(1)$ term)?

I am particularly interested in whether the random-graph that governs the $(1:1)$ game survives in this biased $(2:2)$ setting.

Title: Generalization of the longest chord to $n$-th dimensions
Body:
Recently thinking about the diameter being the longest chord and the great circle is the largest circle inside any given circle and sphere respectively, I wondered if a generalization for any ball of dimension $n$ is possible (it is of course, intuitively, a better way to put it is 'how' it is possible). I managed to put together the question as formally as I could, and got this:

\begin{aligned} &\text{Let } M\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n \text{ be an }n\text{-ball, and let }\Gamma \text{ be the set of flat }(n-1)\text{-balls such that}\\ &\hspace{2cm}N\in\Gamma\implies N\subseteq M.\\[2mm] &\text{Let }\chi(L)\text{ denote the }\dim(L)\text{-hypervolume of }L.\\[3mm] &\text{Now, consider an }(n-1)\text{-ball }K\in\Gamma\text{ such that:}\\[2mm] &\quad 1)\quad \partial L\text{ denotes the boundary of }L\qquad \partial K\subseteq\partial M,\\[2mm] &\quad 2)\quad \exists\,\beta\in K\text{ such that}\\ &\qquad\qquad d(\alpha,\beta) = d(\gamma,\beta) \qquad\forall\,\alpha,\gamma\in\partial M,\\ &\qquad\qquad d(\varepsilon,\beta) = d(\theta,\beta) \qquad\forall\,\varepsilon,\theta\in\partial K.\\[4mm] &\text{Prove that}\\[2mm] &\chi(K)\geq\chi(L),\qquad\forall\,L\in\Gamma. \end{aligned}

Now, many aspects: the hypervolume, the distance function $d: \mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ are not explained for sake of brevity (and because I don't know how to formulate them honestly). I was wondering if any of you would like to give it a shot.

As you can probably tell, condition 1 is essentially that $K$ lies on $M$ instead of in it, and condition 2 is just that $K$ and $M$ are concentric. But I suppose the formalization would help a bit.

If there are any issues with the question, I would appreciate them called out, as I do not have the best track record when drafting questions. Thanks.

Title: Constrained optimisation in half space by log mapping
Body:
I have a non-linear optimisation problem with very expensive function evaluations. Namely, for some admissible set $\mathcal{A}:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^N|\ i=1,\dots,N;\ x>0 \text{ component-wise} \}$ and $f:\mathcal{A}\to \mathbb{R}$ I seek $$\min_{x\in\mathcal{A}} f(x).$$

I am sure that the minimum is not on the boundary of $\mathcal{A}$, because those values make no sense in the context of the problem.

Is there anything wrong simply mapping the admissible set to $\mathbb{R}^N$ via a log function and optimising there? If I define $g(x):=\log x$ then $\mathcal{A}^{\text{log}}:=\{g(x)|\ x\in\mathbb{A}\ \} $, again component-wise log, then I don't have to enforce any active sets or penalties at all. I can just solve:

$$\min_{y\in \mathcal{A}^{\text{log}}} f \circ g^{-1} (y)$$

with gradients $\nabla(f\circ g^{-1})(y)=\nabla f\cdot(\nabla (g^{-1})(y))$.

I don't see this method proposed in any text books, so I guess there must be a drawback I am missing. The upside is not needing to implement constraint processing at all.

Title: Pro-$p$ completion of a pro-finite group

I guess here I am assuming that the inclusion map $\iota: SL_n(\mathbb Z) \to \widehat{SL_n(\mathbb Z)} $ takes $\Gamma_n(m)$ to its profinite completion. Why is that true?

And from here, the pro-$p$ completion should be the maximal pro-$p$ quotient of $\widehat{ \Gamma_n(m)}$ by the universal property of the pro-$p$ completion. $\Gamma_n(p^k)$ is pro-$p$. Now I want to say that there is no other pro-$p$ quotient coming from other factors $SL_n(\mathbb Z_q, b)$. Title: When is a cardinal large enough to imply a strong form of SCH?
Body:
The singular cardinals hypothesis, henceforth SCH, states that if $\kappa$ is a singular strong limit cardinal (i.e., cf($\kappa$) < $\kappa$ and for all $\lambda < \kappa, 2^\lambda < \kappa$), then $2^\kappa = \kappa^{+}$, where $\kappa^{+}$ denotes the successor cardinal of $\kappa$. SCH is a pretty natural axiom to think of partly due to its connections with large cardinals, with the one that sparked my curiosity being the following.

If $\mu$ is strongly compact and $\nu > \mu$ is a singular strong limit, then $2^\nu = \nu^{+}$. That is, SCH holds above a strongly compact cardinal.

I, however, have been wondering how important the strong limit part is. Define the following axiom, the super singular cardinals hypothesis (sSCH):

(sSCH) If $\kappa$ is a singular cardinal, then $2^\kappa = \kappa^{+}$.

Clearly, sSCH follows from GCH, but this isn't extremely important. My main interest is in the large cardinal side of things, which leads me to the question:

Is there any large cardinal property A that implies that if $\kappa$ is an A-cardinal, then sSCH holds above $\kappa$?

I'm looking for nontrivial properties. For example, "$\kappa$ is the least inaccessible cardinal such that sSCH holds above it" would imply sSCH holds above $\kappa$, but this is a trivial and uninteresting example.

Title: There do not exist three integers $n$, $n+2$ and $n+4$, all of which are primes
Body:
I am taking a proofs course and have come across the following statement in my textbook:

There do not exist three integers $n$, $n+2$ and $n+4$, all of which are primes.

Proof:

Assume, to the contrary, that there exist three integers $n$, $n+2$ and $n+4$, all of which are primes. We can write $n$ as $3q$, $3q + 1$ or $3q + 2$, where $q\in\mathbb{Z}$. We consider these three cases.

Case 1. $n = 3q$. Then $3 | n$ and so n is not prime. This is a contradiction.

Case 2. $n = 3q + 1$. Then $n + 2 = 3q + 3 = 3(q + 1)$. Since $q + 1$ is an integer, $3 | (n + 2)$ and so $n + 2$ is not prime. Again, we have a contradiction.

Case 3. $n = 3q + 2$. Hence, we have $n + 4 = 3q + 6 = 3(q + 2)$. Since $q + 2$ is an integer, $3 | (n + 4)$ and so $n + 4$ is not prime. This produces a contradiction.

But it’s obvious that when $n=3$ the cases hold since the sequence 3, 5 and 7 are prime. There is no restriction on $q$, so $q$ could be 0, 2 and 1 for $3q$, $3q+1$, $3q+2$ respectively. Was this an oversight by the author or am I mistaken?

Textbook: Mathematical Proofs: A Transition to Advanced Mathematics; Fourth Edition (pg. 324)

Title: Parametric solutions to simultaneous Diophantine equations $w^3+x^3+y^3+z^3=1$ and $w+x+y+z=1$?

This question relates to the simulteaneous Diophantine equations:

$$w+x+y+z=1 \tag{1a}$$

$$w^3+x^3+y^3+z^3=1 \tag{1b}$$

A recent question concerned the equivalent equations with five terms instead of four, and the answer by Myungheon Lee gave a parametric solution yielding an infinity of numerical solutions. $$v+w+x+y+z=0 \tag{2a}$$

$$v^3+w^3+x^3+y^3+z^3=0 \tag{2b}$$

Clearly, any solution of (1a/b) will immediately provide a solution of (2a/b) simply by putting $v=-1$. (The converse does not hold since many solutions of (2a/b) will not have $-1$ or $1$ as a term.)

Question Do there exist parametric solutions of (1a/b) yielding an infinity of numerical solutions?

Title: Tao's Analysis 4th edition, Exercise 5.4.3, the existence and uniqueness of an integer part of a real number
Body:
In Tao's Analysis the 4th edition, Exercise 5.4.3 asks you to prove that for every real number $x$, there is a precisely one integer $N$ such that $N \leq x < N + 1$.

Please help me complete and potentially correct the following proof.

Proof.

1. The existence.

Let $x$ be arbitrary real number and suppose this $x$ is represented by a Cauchy sequence $(a_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}$ of rational numbers. Choose $\epsilon = 1/2$, then since the sequence is eventually $1/2$-steady, choose a natural number $M$ such that $\forall n, m \geq M: \ |a_n - a_m| \leq \epsilon = 1/2$.

Let's fix $m = M$, then we obtain $\forall n \geq M: \ |a_n - a_M| \leq 1/2$, and then $\forall n \geq M: -1/2 \leq a_n - a_M \leq 1/2$, and finally $\forall n \geq M: a_M -1/2 \leq a_n \leq a_M + 1/2$. In other words, $\forall n \geq M: a_n \in [a_M - 1/2; a_M + 1/2]$.

By Proposition 4.4.1, let's choose a unique integer $N_0$ such that $N_0 \leq a_M - 1/2 < N_0 + 1$ [Basically, at this point, in text we've already showed that such a unique integer exists for a rational number]. Then one obtains $\forall n \geq M: N_0 \leq a_n < N_0 + 2$, which is the same as saying $\forall n \geq M: ((N_0 \leq a_n < N_0 + 1) \ \vee \ (N_0 + 1 \leq a_n < N_0 + 2))$.

[Here is the part where I am lost. Specifically, I don't see why I am allowed to move to an inequality of the form $N_0 \leq x < N_0 + 2$. Furthermore, even if I am allowed to conclude that $N_0 \leq x < N_0 + 2$, it's not clear for me what to do next.]

2. The uniqueness.

The uniqueness follows from the unique choice of $N_0$.

Title: Expectation of a discrete random variable when $\sum_x |x|P(X = x) = \infty$ but $\sum_x xP(X = x) < \infty$.

By the measure-theoretical definition, the mean of $X$ doesn't exist because $E|X| = \infty$. But since $\sum_n x_n\cdot P(X = x_n) < \infty$, I think intuitively the mean exists?

Title: Infinitely many coin flips (or die rolls, etc.)
Body:
Suppose that we have a sample space of infinitely many fair coin flips and the event

$$A_n = \{\text{The first $n$ flips are heads}\}.$$

This event has probability

$$P\{A_n\} = 2^{-n}.$$

Similarly, if we have an event

$$B_n = \{\text{The first tails occurs on the $n$th flip}\},$$

the probability is also

$$P\{B_n\} = 2^{-n}.$$

The part that confuses me (and for which I still haven't found a good answer) is why we're allowed to disregard the flips that occur after the $n$th flip (ie. no matter what we observe afterward, the probability of having the first tails occur on the $n$th flip is $2^{-n}$).

There are several scenarios where this issue is relevant beyond coin flips (observing the first occurrence of a particular number in a die roll, the first occurrence of a particular digit in a real number, etc.) but the intuition eludes me. Would anyone like to explain?

Title: Is the dual module of any proper epimorphic image of an integral domain always zero?
Body:
Given an epimorphism $f:R \to S$ in the category of commutative rings where $R$ is an integral domain, is $\mathrm{Hom}_R(S,R)$ (the module of $R$-linear maps $S \to R$) always the zero module if $f$ is not an isomorphism? If not, is the statement true if $\bigcap_{n \ge 0} a^nR=0$ for every nonunit $a \in R$?

This statement is true if $f$ is the embedding of $R$ into its field of fractions (see For which rings $R$ is $\mathrm{Hom}_R(\mathrm{Frac}(R),R)$ trivial?). It is also true if $f$ is the quotient map $R \to R/I$ for some nonzero ideal $I$ of $R$, as $\mathrm{Hom}_R(R/I,R)$ is isomorphic to the annihilator of $I$, which is zero since $R$ is an integral domain.

If $S$ is the localization of $R$ at some multiplicative set of "denominators" $D$ (and $f$ is the canonical map), then $\mathrm{Hom}_R(S,R)$ is isomorphic to the intersection of the principal ideals generated by the elements of $D$. So, if $\bigcap_{n \ge 0} a^nR=0$ for every nonunit $a \in R$, then the statement holds at least for localizations.

Title: Lower bound on vector field zeros in a positively invariant surface region via periodic orbit dynamics
Body:
Let $M$ be a compact, orientable $C^1$ surface (possibly with boundary), and let $X$ be a $C^1$ vector field on $M$ generating a flow $\phi_t$.

Suppose $N \subset M$ is a compact, positively invariant region such that every equilibrium-free $\omega$-limit set contained in $N$ is a periodic orbit (Poincaré–Bendixson-type behavior).

Let $Z(X\vert{}_N) = \{ p \in N : X(p) = 0 \}$ denote the set of equilibrium points in $N$, and let $\mathcal P_N$ represent topological or dynamical invariants associated with the set of periodic orbits contained in $N$ (their homology classes, counts, or stability types).

Askings:

  1. Is it possible to derive a non-trivial lower bound of the form

$$\# Z(X\vert{}_N) \ge F(\chi(N), \mathcal P_N)$$ where $\chi(N)$ is the Euler characteristic of $N$, and $F$ is a function depending only on $\chi(N)$ and the periodic orbit data $\mathcal P_N$?

  1. Is it also possible to establish an index summation identity on $N$ of the form

$$\sum_{p \in Z(X) \cap N} \operatorname{ind}_p(X) = \mathcal D_N(X)$$ where $\mathcal D_N(X)$ is defined purely in terms of the Poincaré–Bendixson dynamics along the boundary $\partial N$ and the periodic orbits in $N$?

Title: Is the quadratic deletion bound in the positive-fraction Erdős–Szekeres theorem necessary?
Body:
I had been going through a research paper - Andrew Suk and Ji Zeng, A Positive Fraction Erdős–Szekeres Theorem and Its Applications

This was one of the most interesting questions I found:

Let $f(k)$ be the least integer such that every finite sequence of distinct real numbers can be partitioned into at most $f(k)$ block-monotone subsequences of depth at least $k$, after deleting at most $e(k)$ terms.

Suk and Zeng paper show that one can take $$ e(k)=(k-1)^2 $$ and $$ f(k)=O(k^2\log k). $$

Is the quadratic deletion bound $(k-1)^2$ essentially necessary?

I want to mean that does there exist a constant $c>0$ such that for infinitely many $k$, every such decomposition into block-monotone subsequences of depth at least $k$ requires deleting at least $ ck^2 $ terms?
